questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company uses AWS Organizations with 80 member accounts. Compliance requires that no resources be created outside `eu-west-1` and `eu-central-1` in any account, including by account administrators. Global services such as IAM and Route 53 must continue to work. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Create an IAM policy in every account that denies actions outside the approved Regions, and attach it to all IAM users and roles in each account.
Attach an SCP to the organization root denying actions when `aws:RequestedRegion` is not approved, with `NotAction` exempting global services.
Enable AWS Config rules in every account to detect resources created in other Regions, and send non-compliance alerts to the security team.
Use AWS Control Tower account factory to provision new accounts that are restricted to the approved Regions at creation time.
questions.correct_rationale: SCPs set maximum permissions for all principals in member accounts, including administrators, and a Region condition with exclusions for global services enforces the restriction.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-account IAM policies can be modified by local admins, Config rules detect rather than prevent, and account creation settings don't restrict where resources are deployed.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: An SCP attached to an OU allows `s3:*` actions. A developer in a member account of that OU has no IAM policies attached and receives Access Denied when listing S3 buckets. What is the cause?
options: SCPs must also be attached directly to the developer's IAM user in the account.
The S3 bucket policy is missing a public-access statement for the developer's account.
The SCP must use an explicit Allow naming the specific bucket ARN the developer needs.
SCPs only limit what policies can allow and grant nothing, so the developer needs an IAM policy for S3.
questions.correct_rationale: SCPs define guardrails, and effective permissions require an allow in identity or resource policies within those limits.
questions.distractor_summary: SCPs attach to organizational units or accounts rather than users, public access isn't needed, and a more specific SCP still wouldn't grant permissions.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: An application running in Account A needs to read objects from a DynamoDB table in Account B. Security prohibits sharing long-term access keys between accounts. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An IAM role in Account B that trusts Account A's application role, assumed through sts:AssumeRole.
Create an IAM user in Account B and store its access keys in Account A's application configuration files.
Make the DynamoDB table public so that the application in Account A can read items without credentials.
Copy the table to Account A every night with a scheduled job so reads happen locally in Account A.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account roles provide temporary credentials through STS without sharing long-term keys.
questions.distractor_summary: Access keys are long-lived secrets, DynamoDB tables can't be made public, and nightly copies introduce staleness and duplication.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company engages a third-party monitoring vendor that needs read-only access to its AWS account. The vendor serves many customers using the same AWS account, and the company wants to prevent the "confused deputy" problem in which another customer tricks the vendor into accessing this company's resources. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Create an IAM user for the vendor with read-only permissions and send the access keys to the vendor.
Share the root user credentials with the vendor and protect them with a hardware MFA device.
A read-only IAM role trusting the vendor's account, with a unique sts:ExternalId condition.
Grant the vendor access through a public S3 bucket that holds the account's configuration data.
questions.correct_rationale: Requiring an external ID in the role's trust policy ensures the vendor assumes the role only on behalf of this specific customer, mitigating confused deputy risks.
questions.distractor_summary: IAM users require long-term credentials, sharing root credentials is dangerous, and public buckets aren't access control.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company with 50 AWS accounts wants employees to sign in with their existing Microsoft Entra ID credentials and receive role-based access to specific accounts, with centralized assignment and no IAM users in member accounts. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create IAM users in each account and synchronize the Entra ID passwords to each of them.
IAM Identity Center connected to Entra ID as external identity provider, with permission sets assigned to groups.
Amazon Cognito user pools for the employees, with a role mapping configured in each account.
Share one administrator role's credentials with each team and rotate those credentials every quarter for every account.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM Identity Center federates workforce identities from an external IdP and centrally assigns permission sets across accounts in the organization.
questions.distractor_summary: IAM users per account don't scale and create credential sprawl, Cognito is for customer-facing apps, and shared credentials remove accountability.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company wants developers to create IAM roles for their Lambda functions without involving the security team, but must ensure that developers can never create roles with more permissions than a defined maximum, such as access only to their project's S3 buckets and DynamoDB tables. What should the solutions architect implement?
options: Give developers the AdministratorAccess policy and review every role they create at the end of each week.
Use an SCP that denies all IAM actions for the developers' accounts, users, and roles across the whole organization.
Require developers to use the root user for role creation, with MFA enabled on the root user account.
Allow role creation only when a permissions boundary is attached, enforced through a condition key.
questions.correct_rationale: Permissions boundaries cap the maximum permissions of roles developers create, and conditions ensure the boundary is always attached.
questions.distractor_summary: Administrator access and weekly reviews are too permissive, denying all IAM actions blocks the requirement, and root usage is unsafe.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: An application running on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group must upload files to an S3 bucket. A developer proposes storing an IAM user's access keys in the application's configuration file. What should the solutions architect recommend instead?
options: An IAM role attached through an instance profile, giving the application temporary credentials.
Store the IAM user's access keys in environment variables baked into the AMI used by the group.
Make the bucket publicly writable so that the instances can upload without needing any credentials at all.
Use the root user's access keys, stored in the application's configuration on each instance.
questions.correct_rationale: Instance profiles deliver automatically rotated temporary credentials to applications on EC2 without storing secrets.
questions.distractor_summary: Keys in AMIs or environment variables are long-lived and can leak, public write access is insecure, and root keys should never be used.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company's Lambda functions have broad permissions such as `s3:*` and `dynamodb:*` attached during development. Before production, security wants each function's role reduced to only the actions and resources it actually used over the last 30 days. What should the solutions architect use?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor security checks, which flag overly permissive policies across the account.
Amazon Inspector findings, which scan workloads for vulnerabilities and unintended exposure.
IAM Access Analyzer policy generation, based on CloudTrail access activity for each role.
AWS Config conformance packs, which evaluate role policies against a set of managed rules.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM Access Analyzer can generate least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity for a role.
questions.distractor_summary: Trusted Advisor gives broad checks, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and Config evaluates configuration compliance rather than generating policies.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A data team in Account B needs to read objects in an S3 bucket owned by Account A. Account A's bucket policy allows `s3:GetObject` for Account B's `DataTeamRole`, but the team still gets Access Denied. The bucket uses SSE-S3 encryption. What is most likely missing?
options: The bucket must be made public, because cross-account access needs public read permission on all of the objects.
The identity-based policy on DataTeamRole in Account B must also allow s3:GetObject on the objects.
Account B must enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket before cross-account reads can work.
S3 Object Lock must be disabled on the bucket before the cross-account role can read objects.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account access requires permission on both sides: the resource policy in Account A and an identity policy in Account B. Public access isn't needed, Transfer Acceleration affects speed, and Object Lock doesn't block reads.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: Administrators occasionally need to terminate production EC2 instances and delete production S3 buckets. Security requires that these destructive actions be allowed only when the administrator has authenticated with MFA during the session. What should the solutions architect implement?
options: Enable MFA on the root user only and require it for all sign-in activity.
Create a separate AWS account used only for deletions, with its own administrators.
Use AWS Config rules to detect deletions and notify the security team afterward.
Add IAM policy statements denying these actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false or absent.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM conditions based on MFA presence can deny sensitive actions unless the session was MFA-authenticated.
questions.distractor_summary: Root MFA doesn't cover IAM principals, a separate account doesn't enforce MFA, and Config rules detect rather than prevent.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A startup created its AWS account with the root user and has been using it daily with access keys for automation scripts. What should the solutions architect recommend to secure the root user?
options: Enable MFA on the root user, delete its access keys, and use Identity Center users or roles daily.
Share the root user password with the whole team so that no one is ever locked out of the account.
Rotate the root access keys monthly and keep using them for the automation scripts and daily work.
Disable the root user by deleting the account email address, and use access keys for admin work.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS recommends MFA on the root user, no root access keys, and least-privilege identities for daily use, reserving root for specific account tasks.
questions.distractor_summary: Sharing root credentials and continuing to use root keys are risky, and the root user can't be disabled by deleting the email.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company wants to set up a multi-account AWS environment quickly using AWS best practices, including a centralized log archive account, an audit account, preventive and detective guardrails, and automated provisioning of new accounts with baseline configurations. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create the accounts manually and configure logging, guardrails, and access separately in each one.
Use a single AWS account with many IAM users and separate the teams with IAM policies.
AWS Control Tower, which sets up a landing zone with guardrails and Account Factory.
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with parameters for each environment.
questions.correct_rationale: Control Tower automates a best-practice multi-account landing zone with log archive and audit accounts, controls, and account vending.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual setup is slow and inconsistent, a single account lacks isolation, and Parameter Store stores configuration values.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A mobile app allows users to upload photos directly to S3 from their devices. Each user must upload only to their own prefix in the bucket, and the app must not embed long-term AWS credentials. Users sign in with social identity providers. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Embed an IAM user's access keys in the mobile app and rotate them each time a new release ships.
Amazon Cognito identity pools issuing temporary credentials scoped to each user's own prefix.
Make the bucket publicly writable and rely on randomized object names to separate each user's photos.
Proxy all uploads through an EC2 instance that uses the root user's credentials to write to S3.
questions.correct_rationale: Cognito identity pools exchange authenticated user tokens for temporary, scoped AWS credentials, and policy variables can restrict each user to their own prefix.
questions.distractor_summary: Embedded keys can be extracted, public write access is insecure, and root usage is unsafe.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A security team wants to identify all S3 buckets, KMS keys, IAM roles, and Lambda functions across the organization that grant access to principals outside the organization, and be alerted to new findings. What should the solutions architect use?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks, run across all of the accounts in the whole organization.
Amazon Macie, run against every bucket to classify the sensitive data and flag public buckets.
VPC Flow Logs analyzed with Athena to find traffic leaving to principals outside the organization.
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust, alerting on external access findings.
questions.correct_rationale: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to find resources shared with external principals relative to a zone of trust such as the organization.
questions.distractor_summary: Trusted Advisor cost checks don't analyze sharing, Macie discovers sensitive data in S3, and flow logs capture network traffic.

questions.subdomain: 1.1 Design secure access to AWS resources
questions.question: A company has 200 project teams, each with its own resources. Maintaining a separate IAM policy per team is becoming unmanageable. The company wants a single policy that allows users to manage only resources tagged with the same `Project` value as their own principal tag. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: ABAC with one policy that matches the aws:ResourceTag/Project tag to the principal's Project tag, plus enforced tagging.
Create one IAM group for each team and attach a separate team-specific policy to every group, updating them as teams change.
Give every user a separate AWS account and manage access through cross-account roles assumed from a central account.
Grant all users full access to resources and rely on periodic audits and CloudTrail review to catch misuse afterward.
questions.correct_rationale: ABAC uses tags on principals and resources so that one policy scales across teams automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-team policies are what's unmanageable, per-user accounts are impractical, and full access violates least privilege.

questions.question: A company is deploying a three-tier web application in a VPC across two Availability Zones. Only the load balancer should be reachable from the internet, application servers and databases must not have public IP addresses, and application servers need outbound internet access to download patches. What should the solutions architect design?
options: Place all three tiers in public subnets, then use security groups to restrict access between the tiers.
Place the ALB and application servers in public subnets and the database in a private subnet without NAT.
ALB in public subnets, application and database tiers in private subnets, and one NAT gateway per AZ.
Place all tiers in private subnets, then add an internet gateway route to each private subnet route table.
questions.correct_rationale: Public subnets host internet-facing load balancers, private subnets isolate app and DB tiers, and NAT gateways provide outbound-only internet access per AZ for resilience.
questions.distractor_summary: Public subnets for app servers expose them, and private subnets with IGW routes are effectively public.

questions.question: Application servers in an Auto Scaling group must accept HTTP traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The ALB's IP addresses change over time. How should the solutions architect configure the application servers' security group?
options: Allow inbound traffic from 0.0.0.0/0 on port 80 and rely on the ALB for filtering.
Allow port 80 inbound with the ALB's security group ID as the source.
Allow inbound traffic on port 80 from the ALB's current IP addresses, updating them as they change.
Use a network ACL that allows only the VPC CIDR range inbound on port 80.
questions.correct_rationale: Referencing the ALB's security group allows traffic from any resource in that group regardless of IP changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Opening to the internet is insecure, hardcoded IPs break when they change, and allowing the entire VPC CIDR is broader than needed.

questions.question: A web application in a public subnet is receiving malicious traffic from a specific IP range, `203.0.113.0/24`. The team needs to block this range immediately at the subnet level while allowing all other internet traffic. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Remove the security group rule that allows HTTP traffic so the attack traffic is blocked too.
Add a deny rule for the IP range to the instances' security group, attached to each instance in the subnet.
Detach the internet gateway from the VPC until the attack has ended and traffic has returned to normal.
Add an inbound deny rule for 203.0.113.0/24 to the subnet network ACL, numbered below the HTTP allow rule.
questions.correct_rationale: Network ACLs support explicit deny rules evaluated in rule-number order, so a lower-numbered deny blocks the range before the allow.
questions.distractor_summary: Security groups only support allow rules, removing the HTTP rule blocks everyone, and detaching the IGW takes the application offline.

questions.question: Instances in private subnets upload large volumes of data to S3 through a NAT gateway, which is costly. Security also wants S3 access restricted so that the bucket accepts requests only from the company's VPC. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: S3 gateway VPC endpoint in the private route tables, plus a bucket policy requiring aws:SourceVpce.
Move the instances to public subnets so that they reach S3 directly through the internet gateway.
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration through the NAT gateway to lower the cost of the large uploads.
Create an interface endpoint for EC2 and route the S3 uploads through that endpoint instead.
questions.correct_rationale: S3 gateway endpoints provide private routing to S3 without NAT data-processing charges, and the `aws:SourceVpce` condition restricts bucket access to that endpoint.
questions.distractor_summary: Public subnets increase exposure, Transfer Acceleration still uses the internet path, and an EC2 endpoint doesn't serve S3 traffic.

questions.question: Lambda functions and EC2 instances in private subnets with no internet access must retrieve secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and call AWS KMS. Security prohibits adding a NAT gateway or internet gateway. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Create S3 gateway endpoints for Secrets Manager and KMS in each of the private subnets.
Add an egress-only internet gateway and route the workloads' traffic to it from private subnets.
Interface VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and KMS with private DNS and HTTPS security group rules.
Store the secrets in plaintext environment variables instead of calling the Secrets Manager API.
questions.correct_rationale: Interface endpoints give private connectivity to AWS services such as Secrets Manager and KMS within the VPC. Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, egress-only gateways are for IPv6 internet access, and plaintext secrets are insecure.

questions.question: A public e-commerce site behind an Application Load Balancer is being targeted by SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts, as well as HTTP floods from a few IP addresses. The company wants managed protection with minimal rule writing. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Security group rules that block the attacker IP addresses, updated manually as new ones appear.
A WAF web ACL on the ALB with managed SQL database and core rule sets plus a rate-based rule.
Amazon Inspector on the web servers to find and report web application vulnerabilities regularly.
VPC Flow Logs with Athena queries to find the attacking IP addresses and block them.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests, managed rule groups block common attacks such as SQLi and XSS, and rate-based rules mitigate floods from individual IPs.
questions.distractor_summary: Security groups can't inspect requests or deny, Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, and flow logs analyze traffic after the fact.

questions.question: A financial trading platform uses CloudFront, ALBs, and Elastic IPs. It must be protected against large, sophisticated DDoS attacks, with 24/7 access to AWS DDoS experts during attacks and protection against unexpected scaling charges caused by attacks. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Shield Standard on all resources, which provides automatic protection against common network-layer attacks.
AWS WAF rate-based rules on the CloudFront distribution and ALBs to block floods of requests from single IPs.
Amazon GuardDuty with threat intelligence feeds to detect and alert on suspicious network activity in the account.
Shield Advanced with Shield Response Team access and cost protection for the protected resources.
questions.correct_rationale: Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS detection and mitigation, access to the Shield Response Team, and cost protection for attack-related scaling.
questions.distractor_summary: Shield Standard offers baseline protection without these services, WAF alone doesn't cover L3/L4 attacks, and GuardDuty detects threats rather than mitigating DDoS.

questions.question: A company with 30 VPCs connected through a Transit Gateway must inspect all east-west and outbound internet traffic centrally with stateful rules, intrusion prevention, and domain-based filtering, using a managed AWS service. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A central inspection VPC with AWS Network Firewall and Transit Gateway routes through it.
Security groups in each VPC, with rules written to allow only the traffic the application needs.
AWS WAF web ACLs deployed in each VPC to filter both the internal and the outbound traffic.
Network ACLs in each VPC, with rules that match the destination domain names of the traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Network Firewall provides managed stateful inspection, IPS, and domain filtering, and Transit Gateway routing can steer traffic through a central inspection VPC. Security groups and NACLs lack IPS and domain filtering, and WAF protects HTTP applications rather than VPC traffic.

questions.question: A company operates 60 accounts in AWS Organizations. Security wants to enforce a standard AWS WAF rule set on every ALB and CloudFront distribution, and audit and remediate overly permissive security groups across accounts, including new ones automatically. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Configure WAF and security groups manually in each account and keep a shared checklist for the teams.
Use AWS Config in each account, without any central management of the rules.
AWS Firewall Manager with WAF and security group policies applied across the organization.
Amazon Detective to investigate the activity in each account and apply fixes to the rules.
questions.correct_rationale: Firewall Manager centrally applies WAF, security group, and other firewall policies across accounts and automatically covers new resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual configuration doesn't scale, per-account Config lacks central enforcement, and Detective investigates security findings.

questions.question: A company's internal REST APIs built with Amazon API Gateway must be accessible only from applications in its VPCs, never from the public internet. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create a public regional API protected by an API key and a usage plan for each of the internal teams.
A private REST API reached through an execute-api interface VPC endpoint, with a resource policy.
Use CloudFront in front of a public API and restrict the callers by their source IP address ranges.
Use an edge-optimized API with AWS WAF rules that allow only the company's public IP address ranges.
questions.correct_rationale: Private APIs are reachable only through interface VPC endpoints, and resource policies can limit which endpoints or VPCs can invoke them.
questions.distractor_summary: API keys don't restrict network access, and CloudFront and edge-optimized APIs are publicly accessible.

questions.question: Administrators SSH into EC2 instances through a bastion host with a public IP. Security wants to eliminate open inbound SSH ports and bastions, control access with IAM, and record session activity for audits. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Keep the bastion host but restrict inbound SSH to the office IP address ranges, with logs sent to CloudWatch.
Use EC2 Instance Connect with public IP addresses and open inbound SSH from the office to each instance.
Open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 and rotate the key pairs regularly to reduce the exposure.
Session Manager with the SSM Agent and instance roles, no inbound SSH, and session logs in CloudWatch.
questions.correct_rationale: Session Manager provides IAM-controlled shell access without inbound ports or bastions and can log session activity.
questions.distractor_summary: Bastions and public IPs keep exposure, and opening SSH to the internet is insecure.

questions.question: A security team wants to prevent workloads in VPCs from resolving known malicious domains, such as command-and-control and phishing domains, and to allow only approved domains for certain sensitive workloads. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall with managed domain lists and custom allow and block lists.
Security groups with outbound rules that reference the domain names of the known malicious sites.
AWS WAF web ACLs attached to the VPC to block requests to the known malicious domain names.
Network ACLs blocking port 53 for all of the workloads in the VPCs, with allowed exceptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall filters DNS queries from VPCs using managed and custom domain lists.
questions.distractor_summary: Security groups and NACLs don't filter by domain, WAF protects HTTP endpoints, and blocking port 53 breaks all DNS resolution.

questions.question: A SaaS provider wants to expose its service, which runs behind a Network Load Balancer, to hundreds of customer VPCs in other AWS accounts. Many customers use overlapping CIDR ranges, and the provider doesn't want network-level access to customer VPCs. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: VPC peering with each customer VPC, adding route table entries on both sides.
A Transit Gateway shared with all of the customers through AWS Resource Access Manager.
A PrivateLink endpoint service backed by the NLB, with customers creating interface endpoints.
A public endpoint with IP allowlisting for each of the customer networks.
questions.correct_rationale: PrivateLink exposes a specific service to consumers through interface endpoints, works with overlapping CIDRs, and doesn't grant broader network access.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering and Transit Gateway require non-overlapping ranges and create network connectivity, and a public endpoint is less secure.

questions.question: Instances in a dual-stack private subnet need to initiate outbound IPv6 connections to the internet to download updates, but must not accept inbound IPv6 connections initiated from the internet. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: A NAT gateway configured for IPv6 traffic, with a route to it from the subnet's route table.
An egress-only internet gateway, with an IPv6 default route (`::/0`) from the subnet.
An internet gateway with a route for `::/0` and a security group that allows all inbound IPv6.
A VPC peering connection to a public VPC, with routes sending IPv6 traffic across the peering link.
questions.correct_rationale: Egress-only internet gateways allow outbound IPv6 traffic and block unsolicited inbound IPv6 connections.
questions.distractor_summary: NAT gateways are primarily for IPv4, an internet gateway with open inbound rules allows inbound traffic, and peering doesn't provide internet access.

questions.question: A company is building a customer-facing web application behind an Application Load Balancer. It needs user sign-up and sign-in with MFA and social logins, and wants the ALB to authenticate users before requests reach the application, minimizing custom authentication code. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Build a custom authentication service on EC2 that stores salted password hashes and sends MFA codes by email itself.
Create an IAM user for each customer and attach a policy that allows access to the application.
Use IAM Identity Center for the customers, assigning each customer to a permission set in the account.
Cognito user pools with social identity providers and MFA, integrated through the ALB authenticate-cognito action.
questions.correct_rationale: Cognito user pools provide customer identity with MFA and federation, and ALBs can authenticate users with Cognito before forwarding requests.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom services add effort and risk, IAM users aren't meant for customers, and IAM Identity Center is for workforce access.

questions.question: A healthcare company stores patient records in S3. Compliance requires encryption at rest with keys the company controls, the ability to audit every use of the key, and annual automatic key rotation. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys, which are rotated and audited automatically by the service for you.
Client-side encryption using keys stored on the developers' laptops and copied to the servers when needed.
SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, automatic rotation enabled, and key usage recorded in CloudTrail.
SSE-C with keys supplied on every request by the application, and stored in an on-premises system.
questions.correct_rationale: Customer managed KMS keys give control over key policies and rotation, and each use is logged in CloudTrail.
questions.distractor_summary: SSE-S3 keys aren't customer controlled or individually audited, laptop-stored keys are insecure, and SSE-C requires managing keys outside AWS and supplying them with each request.

questions.question: After a data leak caused by a misconfigured bucket ACL, a company wants to guarantee that no S3 bucket or object in its account can be made public, regardless of bucket policies or ACLs that users might add in the future. What should the solutions architect do?
options: S3 Block Public Access at the account level, protected from being disabled by an SCP.
Review all bucket policies and ACLs monthly and fix any that allow public access.
Enable default encryption on all buckets and require TLS in each bucket policy.
Enable S3 Versioning on all buckets so that earlier object versions can be restored.
questions.correct_rationale: Account-level Block Public Access overrides public ACLs and policies for all buckets, and an SCP can prevent it from being turned off.
questions.distractor_summary: Monthly reviews are reactive, encryption doesn't prevent public access, and versioning protects against overwrites.

questions.question: Multiple partner accounts upload objects into a company's S3 bucket. The company has discovered that it can't read some uploaded objects because they're owned by the uploading accounts through ACLs. The company wants to own all objects in the bucket and manage access only through policies. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that the previous object versions can be restored by the owner and read.
Require partners to use SSE-KMS and update the key policy so that the bucket owner can decrypt all uploads.
Enable Requester Pays so that partners are charged for the requests made to the bucket.
S3 Object Ownership set to Bucket owner enforced, which disables ACLs so the bucket owner owns all objects.
questions.correct_rationale: Bucket owner enforced disables ACLs so that the bucket owner automatically owns every object and access is controlled by policies.
questions.distractor_summary: Versioning, encryption, and Requester Pays don't change object ownership.

questions.question: A brokerage firm must keep trade records in S3 in a write-once, read-many (WORM) manner for seven years to meet SEC regulations. No user, including the root user, may delete or overwrite the records before the retention period ends. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: S3 Versioning with MFA Delete enabled, so that deletions require an additional authentication code.
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention period for the trade records.
S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a seven-year retention period set.
A bucket policy denying s3:DeleteObject for all principals on the trade record objects.
questions.correct_rationale: Compliance mode Object Lock prevents any user, including root, from deleting or changing locked object versions until retention expires.
questions.distractor_summary: MFA Delete and bucket policies can be changed by privileged users, and governance mode can be bypassed with special permissions.

questions.question: A security audit requires that all access to a sensitive S3 bucket occur over encrypted connections. Some legacy clients still use plain HTTP. What should the solutions architect add?
options: Enable default encryption on the bucket so that all objects are encrypted at rest with KMS.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket for the clients that use plain HTTP.
A bucket policy that denies all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false.
A lifecycle rule for the bucket that expires objects uploaded over unencrypted connections.
questions.correct_rationale: Denying requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is false enforces HTTPS (TLS) for all access.
questions.distractor_summary: Default encryption addresses data at rest, Transfer Acceleration improves speed, and lifecycle rules manage object transitions.

questions.question: Account A encrypts objects in its S3 bucket with a customer managed KMS key. A role in Account B has an IAM policy allowing `s3:GetObject` and `kms:Decrypt`, and the bucket policy allows the role to read objects, but downloads fail with a KMS access error. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Update the KMS key policy in Account A to let the role in Account B decrypt with the key.
Switch the bucket default encryption to SSE-S3 so that no KMS key is needed for reads.
Make the objects public so the role in Account B can download them without KMS access.
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy the encrypted objects into Account B's bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-account KMS use requires the key policy in the owning account to allow the external principal, in addition to the principal's IAM permissions.
questions.distractor_summary: Changing encryption type weakens control, public objects are insecure, and replication doesn't grant key access.

questions.question: A bank must store encryption keys in single-tenant hardware security modules that it exclusively controls, validated to FIPS 140 Level 3, and use them with Oracle Transparent Data Encryption on EC2 via standard PKCS#11 interfaces. AWS personnel must not be able to access the keys. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS KMS with AWS managed keys, rotated and managed by AWS.
AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation of the keys stored as secrets.
SSE-S3 with S3 bucket keys enabled on the bucket.
AWS CloudHSM, which provides single-tenant HSMs the bank controls exclusively.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudHSM provides dedicated, customer-controlled HSMs with standard interfaces such as PKCS#11 for applications like Oracle TDE. KMS AWS managed keys aren't exclusively customer-controlled, Secrets Manager stores secrets rather than providing HSMs, and SSE-S3 is S3 encryption.

questions.question: An application connects to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database using a password stored in a configuration file. Security requires that the password be stored securely, rotated automatically every 30 days, and retrieved by the application at runtime without code changes at each rotation. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Store the password in an S3 object encrypted with SSE-KMS and have an administrator rotate it by hand each quarter.
Secrets Manager with automatic rotation for the RDS database, retrieved by the application at runtime.
Hardcode the password in the AMI and rebuild the AMI and the launch template whenever it has to change.
Store the password in an EC2 user data script that runs when each of the instances launches, encrypted at rest.
questions.correct_rationale: Secrets Manager stores credentials encrypted and supports automatic rotation for RDS, with applications fetching current values at runtime.
questions.distractor_summary: S3 objects and manual rotation lack integration, and hardcoding in AMIs or user data exposes the password.

questions.question: An application needs to store 200 configuration values, such as feature flags and endpoint URLs, and a few API tokens that don't need automatic rotation. The team wants a low-cost, hierarchical store with encryption for sensitive values and IAM-based access. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Secrets Manager for all of the values, including the feature flags and the endpoint URLs, with rotation.
DynamoDB with no encryption, with the values loaded into the application at startup.
Systems Manager Parameter Store, with SecureString parameters encrypted with KMS for the tokens.
Environment variables baked into the container images and rebuilt for each release.
questions.correct_rationale: Parameter Store provides hierarchical, low-cost configuration storage with KMS-encrypted SecureString parameters and IAM access control.
questions.distractor_summary: Secrets Manager costs more per secret and its rotation features aren't needed here, unencrypted DynamoDB doesn't protect tokens, and baked-in variables are hard to change and can leak.

questions.question: A company's security policy requires that every new EBS volume and snapshot in its AWS accounts be encrypted, but developers sometimes forget to select encryption when launching instances. What should the solutions architect do?
options: EBS encryption by default in each Region of every account, with the KMS key to use specified.
Ask developers to use a checklist when they create the volumes, and audit the results monthly.
Encrypt each volume manually after launch by copying its snapshot with encryption enabled each time.
Use instance store volumes instead of EBS volumes for all of the instances in the accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: EBS encryption by default ensures new volumes and snapshots are encrypted automatically in that Region.
questions.distractor_summary: Checklists are unreliable, existing unencrypted volumes can't be encrypted in place, and instance store is ephemeral and not a replacement.

questions.question: A company discovers that an existing production Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance was created without encryption at rest. Compliance now requires encryption. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable encryption on the running instance through the console, which applies it after a short reboot.
Enable EBS encryption by default in the Region, which then also encrypts the existing instance's volumes.
Enable SSL connections to the database and require them for all of the clients in the parameter group.
Copy a snapshot with encryption using a KMS key, restore from it to a new instance, then cut over.
questions.correct_rationale: Encryption can't be enabled on an existing unencrypted RDS instance, but an encrypted copy of a snapshot can be restored to a new encrypted instance.
questions.distractor_summary: EBS default encryption doesn't apply to existing RDS storage, and SSL encrypts data in transit rather than at rest.

questions.question: A company serves its website through CloudFront with a custom domain and an Application Load Balancer origin in `eu-west-1`. It wants free, automatically renewing TLS certificates for both CloudFront and the ALB. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Request one ACM certificate in eu-west-1 and use it for CloudFront and the ALB.
A public ACM certificate in us-east-1 for CloudFront and another in eu-west-1 for the ALB.
Upload self-signed certificates to IAM and attach them to the distribution and the ALB.
Purchase certificates from a third party and renew them manually before each one expires.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudFront requires ACM certificates in `us-east-1`, while ALBs use certificates in their own Region, and public ACM certificates are free and renew automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: A single Regional certificate can't be used by CloudFront, self-signed certificates cause browser errors, and third-party certificates require manual renewal.

questions.question: A shared S3 bucket holds a large dataset used by 25 applications, each needing different permissions to different prefixes. The single bucket policy has become too complex to manage, and some applications must access the data only from within a specific VPC. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create 25 copies of the bucket, one for each application, and sync the data between the copies nightly using replication.
Use IAM users with access keys for each application, with inline policies limited to its prefix.
S3 Access Points for each application, each with its own policy and VPC-only network origin if needed.
Make the bucket public and rely on hard-to-guess prefix names to limit each application's view.
questions.correct_rationale: Access points simplify managing access to shared datasets by giving each application its own endpoint and policy, and they can be restricted to a VPC. Copies duplicate data, access keys add credential risk, and public access is insecure.

questions.question: A document portal stores invoices in a private S3 bucket. Customers must be able to download their own invoice from a link that works for 15 minutes, without having AWS credentials and without making objects public. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Generate S3 presigned URLs in the backend with a 15-minute expiration.
Make the invoices public and use long random object names so that links are hard to guess.
Create an IAM user for each customer and give each one read access to their own invoice.
Email the invoice files as attachments directly from S3 whenever a customer asks for one.
questions.correct_rationale: Presigned URLs grant time-limited access to specific objects using the application's credentials.
questions.distractor_summary: Public objects with obscure names are insecure, IAM users per customer don't scale, and S3 doesn't send emails.

questions.question: A government contractor's compliance framework requires that data stored in S3 be protected with two independent layers of encryption applied at the object level, managed through AWS KMS. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: SSE-S3 with S3 bucket keys enabled, applied once to every object stored in the bucket.
SSE-C with client-supplied keys, with the key sent by the client on every request to S3.
Client-side encryption done by the application on each object before it is uploaded.
Dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (DSSE-KMS) on the S3 bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: DSSE-KMS applies two layers of encryption to objects using KMS-managed keys, meeting dual-layer requirements.
questions.distractor_summary: SSE-S3 and SSE-C provide a single layer, and client-side encryption alone doesn't provide the specified server-side dual layer.

questions.question: A company with 70 accounts in AWS Organizations must retain a tamper-evident record of all management API activity in every account and Region for seven years, stored centrally where member account administrators can't delete or modify it. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable CloudTrail separately in each account, with the logs stored locally in a bucket in that account and reviewed monthly.
An organization trail logging all Regions to a log archive account bucket, with integrity validation and Object Lock.
Use VPC Flow Logs in every VPC and send the logs to a central CloudWatch Logs log group for later analysis by the team.
Rely on the 90-day CloudTrail event history in each account and have the teams export the events by hand once every year or so.
questions.correct_rationale: An organization trail captures activity across all accounts and Regions, centralizing logs in a protected archive account with integrity validation and Object Lock.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-account local logs can be altered by local admins, flow logs record network traffic, and event history lasts only 90 days.

questions.question: A company wants continuous threat detection across all accounts in its organization, including detection of compromised credentials used from unusual locations, EC2 instances communicating with cryptocurrency mining pools, and anomalous S3 data access, with minimal setup. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: GuardDuty across the organization through a delegated administrator, with auto-enable for new accounts.
Amazon Inspector enabled to scan the instances for software vulnerabilities and exposure.
AWS Config managed rules that check the resources for compliance with the security baseline.
AWS Trusted Advisor checks of the security category in each of the accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and other sources to detect threats, and it can be managed organization-wide with auto-enable.
questions.distractor_summary: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, Config evaluates configuration compliance, and Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks.

questions.question: A security team receives findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and Firewall Manager in 40 accounts across four Regions. It wants a single view of prioritized findings, automated checks against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices and CIS benchmarks, and aggregation into one Region. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon Detective behavior graphs that combine the findings from the services into a single view.
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards in each account that show the findings from each of the services.
Security Hub with a delegated administrator, security standards enabled, and cross-Region aggregation.
AWS Artifact reports downloaded from each account and then combined by hand by the security team.
questions.correct_rationale: Security Hub aggregates findings from AWS security services across accounts and Regions and runs automated standards checks.
questions.distractor_summary: Detective investigates findings, CloudWatch dashboards aren't a findings aggregator, and Artifact provides compliance reports from AWS.

questions.question: A company must detect S3 buckets that have default encryption disabled or public access allowed, and automatically correct these misconfigurations within minutes, while keeping a history of configuration changes for audits. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A monthly manual review of all of the buckets, with fixes applied by the storage team.
Amazon Macie scans of all the buckets, with findings sent to the security team to fix.
Amazon Inspector scans of the buckets, with the findings sent to the storage team.
AWS Config managed rules for S3 encryption and public access, with automatic remediation through SSM Automation.
questions.correct_rationale: Config continuously evaluates resource configurations, records change history, and can trigger automatic remediation via Systems Manager Automation.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual reviews are slow, Macie discovers sensitive data, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities.

questions.question: After an acquisition, a company inherited 400 S3 buckets and doesn't know which contain personally identifiable information such as credit card numbers and passport numbers. Compliance requires an inventory of sensitive data and alerts when it appears in unexpected buckets. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Config rules that evaluate the buckets for the presence of credit card numbers.
Amazon Macie with automated sensitive data discovery across the buckets.
Amazon GuardDuty S3 protection, which detects PII in the objects of the buckets.
S3 Storage Lens dashboards showing the PII in the buckets.
questions.correct_rationale: Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and report sensitive data in S3.
questions.distractor_summary: Config evaluates configurations rather than content, GuardDuty detects threats rather than classifying data, and Storage Lens reports usage and activity metrics.

questions.question: A company wants continuous vulnerability scanning of its EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR, and Lambda functions, with findings prioritized by risk and updated automatically when new CVEs are published. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon Inspector, enabled across the organization with a delegated administrator.
Amazon GuardDuty, enabled across the organization to analyze logs for threats.
AWS Shield Advanced, enabled across the organization for DDoS protection.
AWS WAF with managed rule groups, applied to the organization's public endpoints.
questions.correct_rationale: Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and network exposure, and re-evaluates as new CVEs appear.
questions.distractor_summary: GuardDuty detects threats, Shield mitigates DDoS, and WAF filters HTTP requests.

questions.question: GuardDuty reported that an IAM role was used to make unusual API calls. The security team needs to investigate the root cause quickly, visualizing related entities such as IP addresses, users, roles, and EC2 instances, and their activity over time, without building custom queries. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Config timeline of the changes to the role's configuration and related resources.
Amazon Macie to classify the data that the role accessed during the unusual API calls.
Amazon Detective, using behavior graphs linked from the GuardDuty finding.
AWS Trusted Advisor security checks of the account, with recommended fixes for the role.
questions.correct_rationale: Detective builds behavior graphs from log data to help investigate the scope and root cause of security findings.
questions.distractor_summary: Config tracks resource configuration changes, Macie discovers sensitive data, and Trusted Advisor provides best-practice checks.

questions.question: When GuardDuty detects that an EC2 instance is communicating with a known command-and-control server, the security team wants the instance automatically isolated within minutes and the team notified, while preserving the instance for forensics. What should the solutions architect design?
options: Terminate the instance automatically using an Auto Scaling policy, and launch a replacement instance in the same Availability Zone.
Review the GuardDuty findings in the console every day and isolate any affected instances by hand.
Disable GuardDuty to stop false positives, then rely on security group rules for the instances.
An EventBridge rule on the GuardDuty finding invoking Lambda to isolate the instance, snapshot it, and notify SNS.
questions.correct_rationale: EventBridge rules on GuardDuty findings enable automated containment that isolates the instance while preserving evidence.
questions.distractor_summary: Termination destroys evidence, daily reviews are too slow, and disabling detection removes visibility.

questions.question: Auditors want to run SQL queries over five years of CloudTrail activity across the organization, for example to find every IAM policy change by a specific user, without the company managing S3 partitions, Glue tables, or Athena configuration. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: CloudTrail event history in the console, filtered by event name and by the name of the IAM user.
CloudTrail Lake with an organization event data store and an appropriate retention period.
VPC Flow Logs in CloudWatch Logs, queried with Logs Insights to find every IAM policy change.
AWS Config advanced queries over the configuration items for the last five years.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudTrail Lake stores events in managed event data stores with long retention and supports SQL queries directly.
questions.distractor_summary: Event history covers only 90 days, flow logs contain network data, and Config queries cover resource configurations rather than API activity.

questions.question: To meet CIS benchmark requirements, the security team must receive an alert within minutes whenever the root user signs in or someone makes unauthorized API calls in an account. CloudTrail already delivers logs to CloudWatch Logs. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: CloudWatch Logs metric filters for root sign-ins and unauthorized API calls, with alarms notifying SNS.
A weekly Athena query on the CloudTrail logs, with the results sent by email to the whole security team.
AWS Trusted Advisor notifications for the security checks, delivered by email to the account owner weekly.
S3 event notifications on the CloudTrail bucket that send an email whenever a log file is written.
questions.correct_rationale: Metric filters convert matching log events into metrics, and alarms send near-real-time notifications.
questions.distractor_summary: Weekly queries are too slow, Trusted Advisor doesn't alert on these events, and S3 notifications fire per log file rather than analyzing content.

questions.question: An EC2 instance in production shows signs of compromise. The incident response plan requires containing the threat while preserving evidence for forensic analysis. What should the solutions architect recommend as initial steps?
options: Terminate the instance immediately, launch a replacement from the AMI, and review the logs later on.
Reboot the instance to clear the malicious processes and then restore normal traffic to the instance.
Isolate the instance with a restrictive security group, deregister it from the ALB and Auto Scaling, and snapshot the EBS volumes.
Delete the instance's CloudTrail logs to prevent the attacker from reading them or the evidence.
questions.correct_rationale: Containment with isolation and removal from service, combined with evidence preservation through snapshots and memory capture, follows AWS incident response guidance.
questions.distractor_summary: Terminating or rebooting destroys evidence, and deleting logs destroys the audit trail.

questions.question: A developer accidentally committed IAM user access keys with administrator permissions to a public GitHub repository. What should the solutions architect recommend as the immediate response?
options: Delete the GitHub repository and continue using the keys, since the repository is then no longer public to others.
Rotate the keys during the next scheduled maintenance window, then notify the developer about it by email later.
Change the IAM user's console password and enable MFA for that user, but leave the access keys active for now.
Deactivate and delete the exposed keys, review CloudTrail for their use, and move to role-based credentials.
questions.correct_rationale: Exposed keys must be revoked immediately, their use investigated, and damage remediated, followed by eliminating long-term keys where possible.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the repository doesn't revoke keys already copied, delayed rotation leaves them usable, and a password change doesn't affect access keys.

questions.question: A compliance team needs a single view of AWS Config rule compliance and resource configurations across 60 accounts and all Regions in the organization. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Sign in to each account and Region separately and export the rule results into a shared spreadsheet.
An AWS Config aggregator in a delegated administrator account, collecting from all organization accounts and Regions.
Amazon Inspector dashboards in the management account, which summarize vulnerability findings across the organization.
CloudTrail event history in the management account, filtered to the configuration-related API calls.
questions.correct_rationale: Config aggregators consolidate configuration and compliance data from multiple accounts and Regions into one view.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual checks don't scale, Inspector reports vulnerabilities, and CloudTrail history covers API activity rather than compliance status.

questions.question: A security analyst suspects that an EC2 instance has been sending data to an external IP address. The analyst needs to see which instances communicated with that IP, when, and how much data was transferred, and whether the traffic was accepted or rejected. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3, queried for the external IP address.
Enable S3 server access logging on the bucket and query the log files for the external IP address.
Use AWS Config timelines to see which instances connected to the address.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to see which instances connected to the address.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC Flow Logs capture IP traffic metadata, including source, destination, bytes, and accept or reject actions.
questions.distractor_summary: S3 access logs record S3 requests only, Config shows configuration changes, and Trusted Advisor doesn't record traffic.

questions.question: A payments company prepares for an annual PCI DSS audit and spends weeks manually gathering screenshots and configuration evidence from AWS. It wants continuous, automated evidence collection mapped to PCI DSS controls, with audit-ready reports. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Artifact, downloading the AWS compliance reports and sending them to the auditors along with screenshots.
Amazon GuardDuty, exporting the findings from every account and sending them to the auditors each month as evidence.
AWS Audit Manager with the PCI DSS framework, collecting evidence from Config, CloudTrail, and Security Hub.
Amazon Macie, scanning the buckets for card data and sending the findings to the auditors.
questions.correct_rationale: Audit Manager continuously collects evidence mapped to compliance framework controls and generates assessment reports.
questions.distractor_summary: Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports rather than evidence about the company's environment, GuardDuty detects threats, and Macie discovers sensitive data.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: An image processing application has a web tier that accepts uploads and an EC2-based processing tier. During traffic spikes, the processing tier falls behind and the web tier times out waiting for it, causing lost requests. The company wants the tiers decoupled and the processing tier to scale with the amount of pending work. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the web tier's timeout and add more web servers to absorb the traffic during the spikes.
A web tier sending jobs to SQS, with the processing group scaled on backlog per instance.
Replace the processing tier with one larger single EC2 instance to handle the whole peak load.
Use sticky sessions on the load balancer so that each client reaches the same processing server.
questions.correct_rationale: SQS buffers work so the web tier responds immediately, and scaling on queue backlog per instance matches processing capacity to pending jobs.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer timeouts and more web servers don't fix the bottleneck, a single larger instance has limits and no redundancy, and sticky sessions don't decouple tiers.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A banking application processes account transactions. Transactions for each account must be processed in the exact order they were submitted, and no transaction may be processed twice. Transactions for different accounts can be processed in parallel. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An SQS standard queue with the account ID added to each message as an attribute.
An SNS standard topic with one SQS subscription for each of the accounts.
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivering the transactions to a Lambda function.
An SQS FIFO queue using the account ID as the message group ID, with deduplication.
questions.correct_rationale: FIFO queues preserve order within each message group and provide exactly-once processing via deduplication, while different groups process in parallel.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard queues and SNS topics offer at-least-once delivery without strict ordering, and Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations rather than ordered transaction processing.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: When an order is placed, three independent systems (inventory, shipping, and analytics) must each receive a copy of the order event and process it at their own pace. If one system is temporarily down, it must not lose events or affect the others. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An SNS topic with three SQS subscriptions, one per system (fan-out).
Send each order to a single SQS queue that all three systems poll for the messages.
Have the order service call each system's API synchronously and wait for the responses.
Write the orders to an S3 bucket and have each system scan it every hour.
questions.correct_rationale: SNS-to-SQS fan-out delivers a copy of each message to durable per-consumer queues, so consumers process independently and buffer during outages.
questions.distractor_summary: A single queue delivers each message to only one consumer, synchronous calls couple availability, and hourly scans add delay.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: Workers consume messages from an SQS standard queue. Each message takes about 90 seconds to process, but the queue's visibility timeout is 30 seconds. The team notices many messages are processed two or three times. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Switch to long polling so that workers wait for messages and see fewer empty responses, with lower cost.
Decrease the message retention period so that old messages are removed from the queue sooner.
Increase the visibility timeout above the maximum processing time, and make processing idempotent.
Enable server-side encryption on the queue so that messages are not delivered to other workers.
questions.correct_rationale: If processing takes longer than the visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and another worker processes it; a longer timeout plus idempotent processing prevents duplicate side effects.
questions.distractor_summary: Long polling reduces empty receives, retention controls how long messages are kept, and encryption doesn't affect visibility.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A few malformed messages in an SQS queue repeatedly fail processing, are retried indefinitely, and consume worker capacity. The team wants these messages set aside automatically after five failed attempts so they can be inspected later. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Reduce the queue's message retention period to one minute so failing messages expire quickly.
Configure a dead-letter queue with a redrive policy that sets `maxReceiveCount` to 5.
Switch to a FIFO queue so that failed messages are retried in order exactly once.
Purge the queue every day with a scheduled job to remove messages that keep failing.
questions.correct_rationale: A dead-letter queue receives messages that exceed the maximum receive count, isolating poison messages for later analysis.
questions.distractor_summary: Short retention discards good messages too, FIFO doesn't handle poison messages by itself, and purging deletes all messages.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company receives events from a SaaS partner integration, from AWS services such as EC2 state changes, and from its own applications. Different events must be routed to different targets (Lambda, Step Functions, SQS) based on event content, with minimal custom routing code. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: EventBridge event buses with content-based rules routing events to targets, including partner sources.
A custom router application on EC2 that reads all of the events and forwards each to the correct targets.
An SQS queue that all of the targets poll, with each target skipping any events not meant for that target.
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, delivering all of the events to a single S3 bucket for later use.
questions.correct_rationale: EventBridge ingests events from AWS services, SaaS partners, and custom applications, and routes them with content-based rules to many target types.
questions.distractor_summary: A custom router adds maintenance, a shared queue doesn't route by content, and Firehose delivers streams to storage destinations.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: An order workflow must reserve inventory, charge a payment, and create a shipment by calling three services. If a later step fails, previous steps must be undone (for example, releasing inventory and refunding payment). The workflow needs retries with backoff and visibility into each execution's state. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A single Lambda function that calls all three services in sequence and reverses the steps itself on failure.
An SQS queue placed between each pair of the services, with no coordination of the separate steps.
A cron job on EC2 that checks for failures every few minutes and starts the compensating actions by script.
Step Functions Standard workflow with retry policies and catch blocks invoking compensating actions.
questions.correct_rationale: Step Functions coordinates multi-step workflows with built-in retries, error handling, and execution history, enabling saga compensation.
questions.distractor_summary: A single function is hard to make reliable and lacks visibility, uncoordinated queues don't manage compensation, and cron-based checks are slow and fragile.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A Lambda function processes messages from an SQS queue in batches of 10. When one message in a batch fails, the entire batch is retried, causing the other nine successfully processed messages to be reprocessed. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Set the batch size to 10,000 so that failures become rarer within each of the batches.
Increase the Lambda timeout so that every message in a batch finishes in time.
Partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures), returning only the failed message IDs.
Switch to an SNS trigger so that each message is delivered to the function separately.
questions.correct_rationale: With partial batch responses, only failed messages return to the queue, avoiding reprocessing successful ones.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger batch increases the blast radius, a longer timeout doesn't address partial failures, and SNS doesn't provide queue-based retries.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A startup needs a REST API for its mobile app that scales automatically from zero to thousands of requests per second, with request throttling and per-client quotas using API keys, and no servers to manage. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An EC2 Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, with AWS WAF rate-based rules for throttling the requests.
API Gateway REST API with Lambda integrations, using usage plans with API keys for throttling.
A single EC2 instance with Nginx, with rate limiting configured in the web server settings.
Amazon ECS on EC2 with manual scaling, with rate limits applied by the application code itself.
questions.correct_rationale: API Gateway with Lambda provides serverless, automatically scaling APIs, and usage plans enforce throttling and quotas per API key.
questions.distractor_summary: EC2- and ECS-on-EC2-based options require server management, and a single instance lacks scalability and resilience.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A payment service receives requests through a queue with at-least-once delivery, and clients may retry after timeouts. The business can't tolerate customers being charged twice for the same order. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Switch to UDP for faster delivery so that clients are less likely to time out and retry.
Increase the queue's retention period so that the duplicate messages expire before the service processes them.
Disable retries on clients so the payment service never receives a duplicate request.
Make the operation idempotent with an idempotency key, recording processed keys with a conditional write.
questions.correct_rationale: Idempotency ensures repeated requests with the same key produce a single effect, which is essential with at-least-once delivery and retries.
questions.distractor_summary: Transport changes and retention don't prevent duplicates, and disabling retries reduces reliability.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A gaming company streams player events that must be processed in order per player. Four independent applications (fraud detection, leaderboards, analytics, and archival) must each read the full stream with low latency, and the company wants to replay the last 24 hours of events if a consumer has a bug. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Kinesis Data Streams with the player ID as partition key, using enhanced fan-out for consumers.
An SQS standard queue for each consumer, with messages copied into each queue by a function.
Amazon SNS with email subscriptions for each application, delivering every event as an email.
Amazon S3 with event notifications sent to each of the four applications for processing.
questions.correct_rationale: Kinesis Data Streams preserves order per partition key, retains data for replay, and supports multiple consumers, with enhanced fan-out giving each consumer dedicated throughput.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard queues don't guarantee order or allow replay after deletion, SNS email isn't a streaming consumer, and S3 notifications aren't designed for ordered low-latency streams.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company is migrating an on-premises application that uses Apache ActiveMQ with JMS and the AMQP protocol. The company wants a managed message broker on AWS without rewriting messaging code. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon SQS, with the clients rewritten to use the SQS API instead of JMS and AMQP.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, with the clients rewritten to use the Kinesis APIs instead.
Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ, supporting JMS and AMQP without rewriting the clients.
Amazon SNS topics, with the clients rewritten as subscribers of those topics.
questions.correct_rationale: Amazon MQ provides managed ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ brokers that support standard protocols such as JMS and AMQP, avoiding code rewrites.
questions.distractor_summary: SQS, Kinesis, and SNS use AWS-specific APIs that would require changes.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company is splitting a monolith into microservices on ECS: requests to `/orders/*` go to the orders service, `/users/*` to the users service, and `/catalog/*` to the catalog service, all behind a single public endpoint that scales automatically. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A Network Load Balancer with one listener per service, each forwarding to its own target group.
An Application Load Balancer with path-based rules routing to a target group per service.
Three separate public Application Load Balancers, one per service, each with its own DNS name.
Route 53 weighted routing records that send a share of traffic to each service endpoint.
questions.correct_rationale: ALBs support path-based routing to multiple target groups behind one endpoint, integrating with ECS services.
questions.distractor_summary: NLBs operate at Layer 4 without path routing, separate ALBs add cost and complexity, and weighted DNS doesn't route by path.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A development team wants to run containerized microservices on AWS without provisioning, patching, or scaling EC2 instances, while still using ECS task definitions and automatically scaling the number of tasks with load. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon ECS on EC2 with a self-managed Auto Scaling group.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk with a single instance in each environment.
Amazon EC2 instances with Docker installed on each one.
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate with Service Auto Scaling for the tasks.
questions.correct_rationale: Fargate runs ECS tasks without managing servers, and Service Auto Scaling adjusts task counts.
questions.distractor_summary: ECS on EC2 and Docker on EC2 require instance management, and single-instance Beanstalk environments don't scale.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company already runs its workloads on Kubernetes on-premises using Helm charts, custom operators, and Kubernetes-native tooling, and wants to move them to AWS with minimal changes and a managed control plane. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon EKS, with managed node groups or Fargate profiles.
Amazon ECS with Fargate, converting the Helm charts into ECS task definitions.
AWS Lambda functions, rewriting the Kubernetes workloads as event-driven handlers.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk, packaging the containers into Beanstalk environments.
questions.correct_rationale: EKS runs upstream-compatible Kubernetes with a managed control plane, supporting existing Helm charts and operators.
questions.distractor_summary: ECS, Lambda, and Beanstalk would require re-platforming the workloads.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A web application runs on EC2 instances behind an ALB. Traffic varies throughout the day, and the company wants instances automatically added or removed to keep average CPU utilization near 50%, with instances spread across three Availability Zones. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: A single large instance with vertical scaling, resized by hand whenever the traffic pattern changes.
A scheduled action that adds instances at 9 AM and removes them again later in the evening hours.
An Auto Scaling group from a launch template across three AZs, with target tracking at 50% CPU.
Manual instance launches by the operations team whenever the traffic goes up during the day.
questions.correct_rationale: Target tracking policies automatically maintain a metric such as CPU at a target, and multi-AZ Auto Scaling groups improve resilience.
questions.distractor_summary: Vertical scaling has limits and downtime, a fixed schedule doesn't adapt to actual load, and manual launches are slow.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: An online learning platform sees traffic jump sharply every weekday at 8 AM when classes start. Reactive scaling adds instances too late, causing slow responses for the first 15 minutes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the ALB idle timeout so that requests wait longer during the morning traffic ramp.
Predictive or scheduled scaling before the daily ramp, plus target tracking for unexpected changes.
Disable scale-in so that capacity added in the morning stays in place all of the day.
Switch to smaller instance types so that new instances start faster, then add more of the instances.
questions.correct_rationale: Predictive and scheduled scaling provision capacity ahead of known recurring demand, while target tracking handles deviations.
questions.distractor_summary: Idle timeouts don't add capacity, disabling scale-in wastes money, and smaller instances don't solve late scaling.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
