questions.question: Instances in an Auto Scaling group take eight minutes to become ready because they run long initialization scripts and load large caches. During scale-out events, new capacity arrives too slowly. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the health check grace period to 30 minutes so that new instances are not replaced early.
Use Spot Instances for scale-out to make the capacity cheaper and faster to obtain than On-Demand.
Reduce the maximum group size so that fewer slow instances have to be initialized at the same time.
A warm pool of pre-initialized instances kept stopped or running, brought into service quickly.
questions.correct_rationale: Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready, dramatically reducing time to serve traffic during scale-out.
questions.distractor_summary: A longer grace period delays health detection, Spot doesn't reduce initialization time, and a smaller maximum limits capacity.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A web application stores user session data in the memory of each EC2 instance and relies on ALB sticky sessions. When Auto Scaling terminates instances, users are logged out. The company wants instances to be stateless. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Store sessions in a shared store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB, and disable sticky sessions.
Increase the sticky session duration so that users stay on the same instances for longer.
Disable scale-in on the Auto Scaling group so that instances holding sessions stay up.
Store sessions on each instance's EBS volume so that they survive an instance restart.
questions.correct_rationale: Externalizing sessions to a shared store lets any instance serve any user and makes instances disposable.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer stickiness and disabling scale-in don't solve termination issues and waste resources, and per-instance EBS storage is lost when instances are terminated.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A real-time trading gateway uses a custom TCP protocol, needs to handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, and partners must allowlist a fixed IP address per Availability Zone. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An Application Load Balancer, with the partners allowlisting the DNS name of the balancer.
A Classic Load Balancer with a TCP listener and the partner IP addresses allowlisted by hand.
A Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address in each AZ.
Amazon CloudFront with the TCP traffic forwarded to the origin servers behind the distribution.
questions.correct_rationale: NLBs operate at Layer 4 with very high throughput and low latency, and support static Elastic IPs per AZ. ALBs are for HTTP(S), Classic Load Balancers are legacy, and CloudFront is a CDN for HTTP content.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company runs 40 scheduled jobs (cron expressions and one-time schedules) on a single EC2 instance that invokes Lambda functions and Step Functions workflows. If the instance fails, no jobs run. The company wants a managed, highly available scheduler with retries and dead-letter queues. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Add a second EC2 instance running the same cron jobs and a script that fails over between the two instances.
EventBridge Scheduler with schedules targeting the Lambda functions and Step Functions, with retries and DLQs.
Run the cron logic inside a long-running Lambda function that sleeps between job runs and retries on failure.
Use SQS delay queues for all of the schedules, with workers polling for messages when they are due.
questions.correct_rationale: EventBridge Scheduler is a managed, scalable scheduler that invokes AWS targets with retries and DLQs.
questions.distractor_summary: A second instance would run jobs twice, a sleeping Lambda function isn't feasible for long intervals, and SQS delays are limited and not a scheduling system.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: During traffic spikes, a Lambda-backed API scales to thousands of concurrent executions, each opening connections to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database, which exhausts database connections and causes failures. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the Lambda memory size so that each execution finishes faster and holds the connection for less time.
Move the Lambda function out of the VPC so that it can reach the database endpoint over the public internet.
Increase the database's storage size so that it accepts more of the simultaneous connections.
Amazon RDS Proxy to pool connections, with reserved concurrency limiting the function's executions.
questions.correct_rationale: RDS Proxy pools database connections for many Lambda invocations, and reserved concurrency caps how many run simultaneously.
questions.distractor_summary: Memory size and storage don't change connection counts, and moving out of the VPC doesn't address connection exhaustion.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A Lambda function is triggered by S3 `ObjectCreated` events on a bucket to create resized images, and it writes the resized images back to the same bucket. Costs spike, and the function runs in an endless loop. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Write the resized images to a different bucket or to a prefix excluded from the trigger filter.
Increase the function's timeout so that the function can finish processing all of the new objects.
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that earlier versions of each object are kept for later.
Switch to an SQS trigger on the same bucket so that events are queued for the function.
questions.correct_rationale: Writing output to the same location that triggers the function causes recursive invocations; using a separate bucket or filtered prefix breaks the loop.
questions.distractor_summary: Timeouts and versioning don't stop recursion, and routing through SQS still triggers on the same writes.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: An analytics ingestion service must accept a very high and unpredictable message rate. The order of messages doesn't matter, occasional duplicate delivery is acceptable because processing is idempotent, and the team wants the highest possible throughput with minimal configuration. Which queue type should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An SQS FIFO queue, which preserves message order at a limited throughput.
Amazon MQ with a single broker, which handles the messages with limited scaling.
An SQS standard queue, which gives very high throughput with at-least-once delivery.
An SNS FIFO topic, which preserves message order and deduplicates the messages.
questions.correct_rationale: Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, which suits idempotent, order-insensitive workloads.
questions.distractor_summary: FIFO queues and topics have throughput limits to guarantee ordering, and a single broker is less scalable.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: A company is building a customer support chat feature where the server must push messages to connected clients in real time, and clients send messages back over persistent connections. The team wants a serverless solution that scales automatically. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An API Gateway REST API, with the clients polling the endpoint every second for new messages.
An SQS queue for each client, with each client long polling its queue.
An S3 bucket for each conversation, with clients checking for new objects.
API Gateway WebSocket API integrated with Lambda, storing connection IDs in DynamoDB.
questions.correct_rationale: WebSocket APIs maintain persistent, bidirectional connections, and Lambda with DynamoDB manages messaging and connection state serverlessly.
questions.distractor_summary: Polling adds latency and load, per-client queues don't push to browsers, and S3 isn't a real-time channel.

questions.subdomain: 2.1 Design scalable and loosely coupled architectures
questions.question: An IoT platform needs to orchestrate a short workflow (validate, enrich, store) for each of 50,000 events per second. Each workflow completes in under two seconds, and at-least-once execution is acceptable. The team wants the lowest cost for this high-volume orchestration. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Step Functions Express Workflows, built for high-volume, short-duration event processing workloads.
Step Functions Standard Workflows, built for long-running workflows that run for up to a year.
A single EC2 instance running a custom workflow engine for all of the events.
Amazon SWF deciders and workers running on a fleet of EC2 instances for each of the events.
questions.correct_rationale: Express Workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration workflows with at-least-once execution and lower cost per execution.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard Workflows are priced per state transition and suit long-running, exactly-once workflows, a single EC2 instance isn't scalable or resilient, and SWF is a legacy service.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company runs its production application on a single-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. During an AZ outage, the database was unavailable for hours. The company wants automatic failover to another AZ with no data loss for committed transactions and no application changes beyond using the existing DNS endpoint. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create a read replica in another AZ and promote it manually whenever there is an outage.
Take hourly snapshots and restore the latest snapshot into a new instance during an outage.
Convert the DB instance to Multi-AZ with a synchronous standby in another AZ.
Migrate the database to an EC2 instance with an EBS volume and take backups of the volume.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-AZ deployments synchronously replicate to a standby in another AZ and fail over automatically behind the same endpoint.
questions.distractor_summary: Read replicas are asynchronous and require manual promotion, snapshots cause data loss and long recovery, and self-managed databases on EC2 lack managed failover.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company uses RDS for PostgreSQL. It needs automatic failover typically within about 35 seconds and wants the standby capacity to also serve read-only reporting queries rather than sitting idle. The company doesn't want to migrate to Aurora. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster with two readable standby instances in different AZs.
An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment with a single non-readable standby.
A single-AZ instance with three cross-Region read replicas to promote.
An RDS Proxy in front of a single-AZ instance, to speed up the failover.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-AZ DB clusters use two readable standbys and provide faster failover than Multi-AZ DB instances, whose standby can't serve reads.
questions.distractor_summary: Cross-Region replicas don't provide automatic failover, and RDS Proxy doesn't add database redundancy.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company uses Amazon Aurora MySQL with one writer. It wants reporting traffic spread across read replicas in different AZs, and if the writer fails, a specific larger replica should be promoted first. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Separate Aurora clusters in each AZ, with the data synchronized between the clusters by a scheduled job.
An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for Aurora, with the standby serving all of the reporting queries.
A single Aurora replica, with a manual promotion runbook for the case of a writer failure in the cluster.
Aurora Replicas in multiple AZs with the reader endpoint for reports and failover priority tiers.
questions.correct_rationale: Aurora Replicas share cluster storage, the reader endpoint load balances reads, and failover priority tiers determine which replica is promoted.
questions.distractor_summary: Separate clusters don't share data, the Multi-AZ instance model isn't how Aurora provides HA, and manual promotion delays recovery.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company runs its website on EC2 instances behind an ALB in `us-east-1`. If the site becomes unhealthy, visitors should automatically see a static maintenance page hosted in an S3 bucket configured for static website hosting. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Route 53 weighted routing, sending 50% of traffic to the ALB and 50% to the S3 website endpoint at all times.
Route 53 failover routing with a health check on the ALB and the S3 website endpoint as secondary.
Route 53 geolocation routing that sends visitors to the S3 website endpoint based on their location.
Route 53 simple routing with both the ALB and the S3 website endpoint listed in a single record.
questions.correct_rationale: Failover routing sends traffic to the secondary target when health checks on the primary fail.
questions.distractor_summary: Weighted routing sends traffic to both targets continuously, geolocation routes by location rather than health, and simple routing doesn't use health-based failover.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company deploys its application in `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1`, and `ap-southeast-1`. Users should be routed to the Region that gives them the lowest network latency, and traffic should shift automatically away from any Region whose endpoint fails health checks. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Route 53 simple routing with one record listing the three endpoints.
Route 53 geolocation routing without any health checks on records.
Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks on each Regional record.
Route 53 multivalue answer routing that lists one Region only.
questions.correct_rationale: Latency-based routing directs users to the lowest-latency Region, and health checks remove unhealthy Regions from responses.
questions.distractor_summary: Simple routing doesn't consider latency or health, geolocation without health checks can send users to failed Regions, and a single-Region multivalue setup doesn't use the three Regions.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A multiplayer game uses UDP servers in two Regions. Players' clients connect by IP address and can't handle DNS changes quickly because of client-side DNS caching. The company wants static anycast IPs, traffic routed over the AWS global network, and failover between Regions within seconds. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Global Accelerator with endpoint groups in both Regions, using static anycast IP addresses.
Amazon CloudFront in front of the servers, with the clients using the distribution's domain name.
Route 53 failover routing with a 60-second TTL on the records of both Regions.
An Application Load Balancer in each Region with an alias record for the clients.
questions.correct_rationale: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs, supports TCP and UDP, uses the AWS backbone, and fails over quickly without relying on DNS. CloudFront is for HTTP content, DNS failover depends on client caching, and ALBs don't support UDP or provide global static IPs.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A content management system runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs. All instances must read and write the same set of files concurrently through a POSIX file system, and the file system must remain available if an AZ fails. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: An EBS volume attached to each instance, with rsync copying the files between instances.
Amazon EFS with a Regional file system and mount targets in each AZ.
Instance store volumes on each instance, with the content copied to them at launch.
An S3 bucket mounted as a block device on each instance, shared through the bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: EFS Regional file systems store data across multiple AZs and are mountable concurrently from instances in each AZ. EBS volumes with rsync are complex and inconsistent, instance store is ephemeral, and S3 isn't a POSIX block device.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB uses EC2 status checks only. When the web application hangs while the operating system keeps running, instances stay in service and users get errors. What should the solutions architect change?
options: Increase the Auto Scaling group's minimum size so that more instances are available to serve the traffic.
Replace the ALB with an NLB so that the load balancer restarts any application process that hangs or fails.
Enable detailed monitoring for the instances, so that the metrics are published every minute.
Use ELB health checks in addition to EC2 status checks, so instances failing the ALB check are replaced.
questions.correct_rationale: With ELB health checks enabled, Auto Scaling replaces instances that fail the load balancer's application-level checks.
questions.distractor_summary: A larger minimum doesn't replace unhealthy instances, an NLB doesn't change Auto Scaling's health check type, and detailed monitoring only increases metric frequency.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: Private subnets in three AZs all route internet-bound traffic to a single NAT gateway in AZ-a. During an AZ-a outage, instances in AZ-b and AZ-c lost internet access. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance in AZ-a that has a larger instance type.
Add an internet gateway route to the private subnets so that the instances reach the internet.
A NAT gateway in each AZ's public subnet, with each private subnet's route table using its own AZ's gateway.
Increase the NAT gateway bandwidth so that it can carry the traffic of all three AZs.
questions.correct_rationale: NAT gateways are zonal, so one per AZ with AZ-local routing removes cross-AZ dependency.
questions.distractor_summary: A NAT instance in the same AZ has the same issue, IGW routes would make subnets public, and bandwidth doesn't address AZ failure.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: An application uses a single-node Amazon ElastiCache for Redis OSS cluster as a session store. When the node failed, all sessions were lost and users were logged out. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the node size so that the session store is less likely to fail under the load.
A Redis replication group with replicas in other AZs and Multi-AZ automatic failover enabled.
Switch to ElastiCache for Memcached with more nodes, spreading the sessions across the nodes.
Take hourly snapshots of the node and restore the latest one if the node fails.
questions.correct_rationale: Replication groups with Multi-AZ automatic failover promote a replica when the primary fails, preserving data and availability.
questions.distractor_summary: A bigger node is still a single point of failure, Memcached doesn't replicate data, and hourly snapshots lose recent sessions.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: To save costs, a team stored the only copy of critical customer contracts in the S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access storage class. The compliance team is concerned about availability and durability. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to speed up uploads and downloads of the contracts.
Keep One Zone-IA and enable S3 Versioning so that earlier object versions are retained in the AZ.
Move the data to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which keeps the copy in the same single AZ.
Move the data to S3 Standard-IA, which stores objects across multiple Availability Zones.
questions.correct_rationale: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so data can be lost if that AZ is destroyed; Standard-IA and Standard store data across multiple AZs.
questions.distractor_summary: Transfer Acceleration affects upload speed, versioning doesn't add AZ redundancy, and Glacier Instant Retrieval can't be placed in a single AZ, so that option isn't a valid configuration.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company serves a static website through CloudFront from an S3 bucket in `us-east-1`. It wants CloudFront to automatically retrieve content from a replicated bucket in `us-west-2` if the primary origin returns errors or is unavailable. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Two CloudFront distributions in front of two buckets, with Route 53 weighted routing between the distributions.
Increase CloudFront's default TTL to one year so that all of the cached objects are served during an outage.
A CloudFront origin group with primary and secondary S3 origins, failing over on HTTP errors, with CRR.
S3 Transfer Acceleration on the primary bucket, with the viewers reading through the accelerate endpoint.
questions.correct_rationale: Origin groups let CloudFront fail over to a secondary origin on specified errors, and replication keeps content available in both.
questions.distractor_summary: Separate distributions and DNS weighting add complexity without error-based failover, long TTLs don't help uncached content, and Transfer Acceleration affects uploads.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A company runs five critical EC2 instances that act as quorum members in a distributed system. The loss of multiple instances due to a single hardware failure would cause an outage. The company wants each instance on distinct underlying hardware within an AZ. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A cluster placement group, packing the instances close together for low network latency.
A spread placement group, placing each instance on distinct underlying hardware.
A partition placement group with one partition holding all five of the instances.
Dedicated Hosts in the same rack, with all of the instances placed on one host.
questions.correct_rationale: Spread placement groups place each instance on distinct hardware, reducing correlated failures for small numbers of critical instances.
questions.distractor_summary: Cluster placement groups pack instances close together, a single partition shares hardware, and placing hosts in the same rack increases correlated risk.

questions.subdomain: 2.2 Design highly available and/or fault-tolerant architectures
questions.question: A critical application runs in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs and needs six instances to handle peak load. Leadership wants the application to keep serving peak traffic immediately if an entire AZ fails, without waiting for new instances to launch. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Provision capacity so that two AZs carry full peak load, such as nine instances, three per AZ.
Keep six instances and rely on Auto Scaling to replace the capacity after an AZ failure occurs.
Place all six instances in a single AZ so that a failure in another AZ cannot affect the group.
Use Spot Instances for all of the capacity so that more instances can be added cheaply when needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Static stability pre-provisions enough capacity to absorb an AZ loss without depending on scaling actions during an event.
questions.distractor_summary: Relying on Auto Scaling introduces delay and possible capacity shortages, a single AZ has no resilience, and Spot capacity may be interrupted.

questions.question: A company's application has an RTO of four hours and an RPO of 15 minutes. It wants to minimize DR costs in a second Region while keeping core data continuously replicated. Application servers can be launched from AMIs during a disaster. Which DR strategy should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Backup and restore with daily backups copied to the DR Region and restored when needed.
Multi-site active-active with the full workload running in both Regions at the same time.
Warm standby with full-size servers running in the DR Region and replicated data.
Pilot light: replicate core data to the DR Region, with application servers off and launched from AMIs.
questions.correct_rationale: Pilot light keeps critical data live and the rest ready to start, balancing low cost with an RTO of hours and a low RPO. Daily backups miss the RPO, and active-active or full warm standby cost more than needed.

questions.question: A company needs to recover its web application in a second Region within 15 minutes after a regional failure, with an RPO of seconds. Budget doesn't allow full production capacity in two Regions at all times. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Backup and restore, with the backups copied to the DR Region and restored after a failure.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but functional copy in the DR Region, scaled up during failover.
Pilot light, with the application servers launched from AMIs only after a regional failure occurs.
A single Region with Multi-AZ only, relying on the standby in another AZ.
questions.correct_rationale: Warm standby runs a smaller functional environment that can be scaled up quickly, meeting a short RTO without the cost of full duplicate capacity.
questions.distractor_summary: Backup and restore and pilot light typically take longer to recover, and Multi-AZ doesn't protect against a regional failure.

questions.question: A global e-commerce company requires near-zero downtime and serves users from two Regions simultaneously. Its relational data uses Aurora PostgreSQL. It needs fast cross-Region replication with low-latency local reads in each Region, and the ability to promote the secondary Region quickly. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Backup and restore using AWS Backup, with the backups copied to the second Region on a regular daily schedule.
Pilot light with a stopped DB instance in the second Region, started and promoted by the team when a failure happens.
Active-active in both Regions with Aurora Global Database and Route 53 latency routing with health checks.
A single-Region Aurora cluster with Multi-AZ, with snapshots copied to the other Region each night.
questions.correct_rationale: A multi-site deployment with Aurora Global Database provides low-latency reads in each Region, fast replication, and quick promotion, while Route 53 routes users to healthy Regions.
questions.distractor_summary: Backup and pilot light recover too slowly, and a single Region can't survive a regional outage.

questions.question: An internal reporting application has an RTO of 24 hours and an RPO of 24 hours. The company wants the lowest-cost DR solution in another Region. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Backup and restore: nightly cross-Region backups with AWS Backup, and CloudFormation to recreate the infrastructure.
Warm standby, a scaled-down copy of the environment running in the DR Region at all times.
Multi-site active-active, with the full workload running in both of the Regions at once.
Pilot light with continuous database replication to the DR Region and servers launched later.
questions.correct_rationale: Relaxed objectives fit backup and restore, which is the cheapest DR strategy because nothing runs in the DR Region.
questions.distractor_summary: Warm standby, active-active, and pilot light incur ongoing costs that aren't justified.

questions.question: A company with 50 accounts wants centralized backup policies for EC2, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS resources, with copies sent to another Region and a separate account, and backups protected from deletion by anyone, including administrators, until retention ends. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Custom Lambda functions in each account that create snapshots on a schedule and copy them to another Region.
Manual snapshots that each team creates and copies to another Region and account on a regular basis.
AWS Backup with organization backup policies, cross-Region and cross-account copies, and Vault Lock.
S3 Versioning and Object Lock on all buckets, with replication rules to another Region and account.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Backup centrally manages backups across services and accounts, supports cross-Region and cross-account copies, and Vault Lock makes backups immutable.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom functions and manual snapshots lack central governance and immutability, and S3 Versioning covers only S3.

questions.question: A financial application uses Amazon Aurora MySQL in `us-east-1`. The DR requirements are an RPO of about one second and an RTO of about one minute for a regional failure, with a managed failover process. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Aurora cross-Region read replicas created from snapshots and promoted during a regional outage.
Daily snapshots copied to us-west-2 and restored into a new cluster during a regional outage.
A Multi-AZ Aurora cluster in us-east-1 only, with the standby instances serving the failover needs of the cluster.
Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in another Region, using managed failover during an outage.
questions.correct_rationale: Aurora Global Database replicates with typical lag under a second and supports promoting a secondary Region quickly.
questions.distractor_summary: Snapshot-based approaches have large RPOs, and Multi-AZ doesn't survive a regional outage.

questions.question: A global mobile app stores user profiles and preferences in DynamoDB. Users in North America, Europe, and Asia must read and write with single-digit-millisecond latency in their Region, and the app must continue working if one Region fails. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: DynamoDB global tables with replicas in the three Regions.
A single DynamoDB table in us-east-1 with DAX caches for the other two Regions.
DynamoDB point-in-time recovery enabled on the table, with restores into each Region.
DynamoDB exports to S3 with cross-Region replication of the exported files.
questions.correct_rationale: Global tables provide multi-Region, multi-active replication so users read and write locally, and the app continues if a Region fails.
questions.distractor_summary: A single Region with DAX adds latency for distant users and doesn't survive a regional outage, PITR restores within a Region, and S3 exports aren't live databases.

questions.question: A company must replicate new objects in an S3 bucket to another Region for DR, and compliance requires a service-level commitment that 99.99% of objects are replicated within 15 minutes, with metrics and notifications for replication status. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: S3 Same-Region Replication between two buckets in one Region.
S3 Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) enabled.
AWS DataSync tasks scheduled to run every hour between the two buckets.
S3 Batch Operations jobs run daily to copy the new objects across.
questions.correct_rationale: Replication Time Control provides an SLA-backed replication time for most objects within 15 minutes, with metrics and events.
questions.distractor_summary: Same-Region Replication doesn't cover regional DR, and scheduled DataSync or Batch Operations don't meet the 15-minute commitment.

questions.question: A company wants to use AWS as the disaster recovery site for 200 on-premises physical and virtual servers running various operating systems. It needs continuous block-level replication with an RPO of seconds, low-cost staging resources, and the ability to launch recovered servers within minutes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Backup with daily backups of the servers, restored into EC2 during a disaster.
AWS DataSync tasks copying the server files to S3, then rebuilding the servers by hand.
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), with continuous block-level replication.
AWS Snowball Edge devices shipped monthly with the server data.
questions.correct_rationale: Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers to a low-cost staging area and launches recovery instances within minutes.
questions.distractor_summary: Daily backups miss the RPO, DataSync transfers files rather than whole servers, and Snowball shipments are periodic.

questions.question: A company's application runs on EC2 instances built from custom AMIs in `eu-west-1`. For its DR plan in `eu-central-1`, the company wants to be able to rebuild the full environment quickly and consistently. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Rely on the default Amazon Linux AMI in the DR Region and install the application after each launch.
Document the manual build steps in a wiki, and have an engineer follow them during a regional disaster.
Take EBS snapshots but keep them only in eu-west-1, and restore from them when the DR plan is needed.
Copy the custom AMIs to eu-central-1 regularly and define the environment in CloudFormation there.
questions.correct_rationale: AMIs are Regional, so copying them to the DR Region and using IaC enables fast, repeatable rebuilds.
questions.distractor_summary: Default AMIs lack custom configuration, manual steps are slow and error-prone, and snapshots kept only in the primary Region are unavailable during a regional outage.

questions.question: A developer accidentally ran a script that overwrote thousands of items in a production DynamoDB table two hours ago. The company needs to restore the table to its state just before the script ran. What should the solutions architect have enabled beforehand?
options: DynamoDB Streams with 24-hour retention, replaying the old item images over the table.
DynamoDB point-in-time recovery, restoring to a second within the 35-day window.
DynamoDB global tables, restoring the overwritten items from the replica in another Region.
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), restoring the items from the cache.
questions.correct_rationale: PITR enables restoring a table to any point within its retention window into a new table.
questions.distractor_summary: Streams capture changes but aren't a restore mechanism, global tables replicate the bad writes, and DAX is a cache.

questions.question: A company runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in `us-east-1` and needs to be able to restore the database in `us-west-2` to a point in time from the last few days if `us-east-1` becomes unavailable, without running a replica continuously. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Enable cross-Region automated backup replication to us-west-2 so that point-in-time restore works there.
Create a Multi-AZ deployment in `us-east-1`, so a standby takes over if one Availability Zone fails.
Increase the backup retention period in `us-east-1` only, so more recovery points are kept in that Region.
Export the database to CSV files every week and store them in an S3 bucket in `us-west-2`.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-Region automated backup replication copies snapshots and transaction logs to another Region, supporting point-in-time restore there without a running replica.
questions.distractor_summary: Multi-AZ and local retention don't cover regional outages, and weekly CSV exports have a large RPO and lose database structure.

questions.question: A research institute runs tightly coupled computational fluid dynamics simulations using MPI across 64 instances. Performance depends on very low inter-node latency and high throughput. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Launch EFA-supported instances in a cluster placement group in a single AZ.
Spread the instances across three AZs using a spread placement group for resilience.
Use burstable instances in a partition placement group across several AZs.
Use Lambda functions for each simulation step, coordinated by queues.
questions.correct_rationale: EFA provides OS-bypass networking for MPI, and cluster placement groups place instances close together for the lowest latency.
questions.distractor_summary: Spreading across AZs increases latency, burstable instances aren't suited for sustained HPC, and Lambda isn't designed for tightly coupled MPI workloads.

questions.question: A company has trained a deep learning model and needs to run high-volume real-time inference at the lowest cost per inference while maintaining low latency. The model is compatible with the AWS Neuron SDK. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: General purpose M instances, with the model served on the CPUs of the instances.
Memory optimized R instances, with the model loaded entirely into instance memory.
AWS Inferentia-based instances (such as Inf2), built for low-cost inference.
Storage optimized I instances, with the model kept on the local NVMe storage.
questions.correct_rationale: Inferentia-based instances are purpose-built for cost-effective, high-performance ML inference with the Neuron SDK. General purpose, memory-optimized, and storage-optimized instances lack ML accelerators and deliver lower inference efficiency.

questions.question: A Lambda function that performs CPU-intensive image processing is configured with 256 MB of memory and takes 12 seconds per invocation. Memory usage is only 150 MB. The team wants to reduce execution time. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the function's timeout so that the longer processing is allowed to complete.
Increase the function's memory allocation, because Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory.
Enable provisioned concurrency so that the function has more CPU for each invocation.
Move the function into a VPC so that it gets dedicated network and CPU capacity.
questions.correct_rationale: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to configured memory, so more memory speeds up CPU-bound functions and can even reduce cost.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer timeouts don't speed execution, provisioned concurrency addresses cold starts, and VPC placement doesn't add CPU.

questions.question: A latency-sensitive API built with API Gateway and Lambda has occasional response times of several seconds due to cold starts, especially during business-hours traffic spikes. The business requires consistently low latency during business hours. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the Lambda timeout so that the cold starts have time to finish.
Decrease the function's memory so that the initialization of each execution environment is quicker.
Move the function to a larger VPC subnet so that more network interfaces are available.
Provisioned concurrency scheduled with Application Auto Scaling to cover business hours.
questions.correct_rationale: Provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments initialized, eliminating cold starts, and scheduled scaling limits cost to business hours.
questions.distractor_summary: Timeouts and less memory don't address cold starts, and subnet size isn't relevant.

questions.question: A Java-based Lambda function using a large framework has cold starts of about eight seconds because of slow initialization. The team wants to reduce startup latency significantly without paying for always-on provisioned environments. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable Lambda SnapStart for the published function versions of the function.
Increase the timeout to 15 minutes so that the initialization has more time.
Use a larger deployment package so that more of the framework is preloaded.
Switch to an SQS trigger so that the function is invoked from a queue.
questions.correct_rationale: SnapStart snapshots the initialized execution environment and resumes from it, greatly reducing cold start latency for supported runtimes like Java.
questions.distractor_summary: Timeouts, larger packages, and trigger changes don't reduce initialization time.

questions.question: A genomics company runs thousands of containerized batch jobs nightly with varying CPU and memory requirements. It wants jobs queued and scheduled automatically, compute provisioned on demand (preferring Spot capacity), and resources released when jobs finish. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: A fixed fleet of On-Demand EC2 instances running cron jobs to start each of the batch jobs.
AWS Lambda for each job, even for jobs that run for several hours at a time.
AWS Batch with managed Spot compute environments (On-Demand fallback) and job queues.
Amazon EMR with a permanent cluster that runs all of the jobs as steps.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Batch manages job queues, provisions the right compute including Spot, and scales down when idle.
questions.distractor_summary: A fixed fleet wastes capacity, Lambda has a 15-minute limit, and a permanent EMR cluster targets big data frameworks rather than general batch containers.

questions.question: A reporting application runs on a `t3.medium` instance. It performs well for part of each day, then becomes very slow, and CloudWatch shows the `CPUCreditBalance` falling to zero. CPU demand is consistently above the instance's baseline for several hours daily. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Add more EBS volumes to the instance and stripe them, to raise disk throughput during the busy hours.
Move to a fixed-performance instance type such as an M-family type sized for the sustained load.
Reboot the instance every day so that the CPU credit balance resets before the busy hours.
Use a smaller T instance type, so the lower baseline accrues credits more quickly each day.
questions.correct_rationale: Burstable instances throttle to baseline when credits run out, so sustained high CPU calls for fixed-performance instances, with unlimited mode as an option for occasional bursts.
questions.distractor_summary: More EBS volumes don't add CPU, reboots don't restore credits, and smaller instances have lower baselines.

questions.question: A small team wants to deploy a Python web application quickly with load balancing, Auto Scaling, health monitoring, and rolling deployments, without designing the infrastructure themselves, while retaining the ability to access the underlying EC2 instances. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Build the infrastructure manually with individual EC2 instances and install an agent for each.
Amazon Lightsail, with the application deployed on a single instance with a static IP.
AWS Lambda, with the Python web application rewritten to run as individual functions.
AWS Elastic Beanstalk, which handles provisioning, load balancing, Auto Scaling and health monitoring.
questions.correct_rationale: Elastic Beanstalk provisions and manages load balancing, Auto Scaling, monitoring, and deployment strategies while letting teams access underlying resources.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual builds require infrastructure design, Lightsail is simpler but less configurable at scale, and Lambda doesn't provide EC2 instance access.

questions.question: A database on EC2 needs 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s of throughput, but only 200 GiB of storage. The team currently uses gp2 volumes and has overprovisioned storage size to get performance. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: gp3 volumes with 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s provisioned independently of the volume size.
st1 volumes, which provide high sequential throughput at a low cost per GB for the database.
sc1 volumes, which provide the lowest cost per GB and burst throughput for the database.
Keep gp2 and increase the volume size to 4 TiB to reach the IOPS.
questions.correct_rationale: gp3 volumes let you set IOPS and throughput independently of capacity, avoiding overprovisioned storage. st1 and sc1 are HDD volumes for sequential throughput with low IOPS, and scaling gp2 size wastes storage.

questions.question: A mission-critical Oracle database on EC2 requires more than 100,000 IOPS with consistent sub-millisecond latency and the highest EBS durability. Which EBS volume type should the solutions architect recommend?
options: gp3 volumes with provisioned IOPS raised to the maximum and throughput set to the maximum.
st1 volumes striped across several devices for sequential throughput on the database.
io2 Block Express volumes, built for sub-millisecond latency above 100,000 IOPS.
sc1 volumes striped across several devices for low-cost cold storage on the database.
questions.correct_rationale: io2 Block Express delivers very high IOPS, sub-millisecond latency, and the highest durability among EBS volumes. gp3 tops out at lower IOPS, and st1 and sc1 are HDD volumes unsuitable for transactional databases.

questions.question: A log processing cluster on EC2 reads and writes large files sequentially and needs high throughput at low cost per GB. Random I/O performance isn't important. Which EBS volume type should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express, built for the highest random IOPS and lowest latency.
Throughput Optimized HDD (st1), built for large sequential I/O at low cost per GB.
General Purpose SSD (gp3) with maximum provisioned IOPS and throughput for every volume.
Magnetic (standard) volumes, a previous-generation type for infrequently accessed data.
questions.correct_rationale: st1 volumes provide high sequential throughput at low cost for big data and log processing. io2 and high-IOPS gp3 cost more for random I/O performance that isn't needed, and previous-generation magnetic volumes offer lower performance.

questions.question: A distributed NoSQL database replicates data across nodes and needs extremely high random I/O with the lowest latency for temporary and replicated data on each node. Data loss on a single node is tolerated because data is replicated elsewhere. What storage should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon EFS, mounted over NFS on each of the database nodes in the cluster.
Amazon S3, with the database nodes reading and writing the objects directly.
EBS sc1 volumes attached to each node of the cluster and striped together.
Instance store NVMe SSD volumes on storage optimized instances such as the I family.
questions.correct_rationale: Instance store NVMe SSDs provide very high IOPS and low latency, suitable for replicated data that can tolerate node loss.
questions.distractor_summary: EFS and S3 have higher latency, and sc1 is cold HDD storage.

questions.question: A video production company uploads files of 50–200 GB to S3 from its studio over a fast connection. Uploads frequently fail near the end and must restart from the beginning. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: S3 multipart upload, with parts uploaded in parallel and failed parts retried.
Compress the files into a single archive and upload the archive in a single request.
Enable S3 Versioning so that failed uploads can be resumed from the earlier version.
Upload to S3 Glacier Deep Archive directly, so that uploads take less time to finish.
questions.correct_rationale: Multipart upload splits large objects into parts that upload in parallel, retrying only failed parts, which improves throughput and resilience.
questions.distractor_summary: Compression doesn't fix restarts, versioning doesn't affect uploads, and Deep Archive is a storage class rather than an upload mechanism.

questions.question: Customers around the world upload large files to a single S3 bucket in `us-east-1`. Users in Asia and Australia report slow uploads over the public internet. The company wants faster uploads without changing the bucket's Region. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create a bucket in each Region and merge the data between them every night.
Use S3 One Zone-IA so that the objects are stored closer to the users.
S3 Transfer Acceleration, with the clients using the accelerate endpoint.
Increase the bucket's request rate limit so that uploads from Asia are faster.
questions.correct_rationale: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through CloudFront edge locations over the AWS backbone, improving long-distance performance.
questions.distractor_summary: Multiple buckets add complexity, storage class doesn't affect upload speed, and request rates aren't the bottleneck.

questions.question: An analytics application issues tens of thousands of GET requests per second against objects in a single S3 prefix and receives HTTP 503 Slow Down errors during peaks. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Switch to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval to lower the cost of the high read rate.
Spread objects across multiple prefixes to parallelize requests, and add retries with backoff.
Enable S3 Versioning so that the older versions of the objects serve the extra reads.
Move the bucket to another Region that has a higher request rate limit for each of its prefixes.
questions.correct_rationale: S3 supports a high request rate per prefix, so spreading keys across prefixes scales throughput, and backoff handles transient throttling.
questions.distractor_summary: Storage class, versioning, and Region changes don't raise per-prefix limits.

questions.question: A semiconductor company runs HPC simulations that need a parallel file system with sub-millisecond latency and hundreds of GB/s throughput. Input datasets live in S3, and results should be written back to S3. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon EFS Standard, mounted on the compute nodes through mount targets in each Availability Zone.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, shared with the compute nodes over SMB through a file share.
EBS volumes attached to each instance, with the datasets copied from S3 onto every volume.
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket through a data repository association.
questions.correct_rationale: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance parallel file system for HPC that integrates with S3 for importing and exporting data.
questions.distractor_summary: EFS isn't optimized for this extreme throughput, FSx for Windows targets SMB workloads, and per-instance EBS volumes aren't shared.

questions.question: A company is migrating Windows applications that use SMB file shares with NTFS permissions, DFS namespaces, and Active Directory authentication. It needs a fully managed file service on AWS with Multi-AZ availability. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: FSx for Windows File Server in a Multi-AZ deployment, joined to Active Directory.
Amazon EFS with NFS mount targets, accessed from the Windows application servers.
S3 with an S3 File Gateway only, presenting the buckets to the Windows servers.
Amazon FSx for Lustre, linked to an S3 bucket for the shared files.
questions.correct_rationale: FSx for Windows File Server provides native SMB, NTFS ACLs, AD integration, DFS, and Multi-AZ deployments.
questions.distractor_summary: EFS is NFS-based for Linux, File Gateway presents S3-backed shares with different semantics, and FSx for Lustre targets HPC.

questions.question: A company is moving on-premises NetApp storage used by both Linux (NFS) and Windows (SMB) clients to AWS. It wants to keep NetApp features such as SnapMirror replication, snapshots, and storage efficiency, with minimal changes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon EFS, which supports the NFS clients and also the Windows clients through a gateway.
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, mounted by the Linux NFS clients as well.
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, which supports both NFS and SMB with NetApp features.
Amazon S3 Glacier, with the NetApp data restored to a share when it is needed.
questions.correct_rationale: FSx for NetApp ONTAP provides multiprotocol access and NetApp data management features such as SnapMirror and snapshots.
questions.distractor_summary: EFS and FSx for Windows support single protocols without ONTAP features, and Glacier is archival storage.

questions.question: A news website's Amazon RDS for MySQL database is overwhelmed by repeated reads of the same popular articles, causing high latency. Writes are infrequent. The company wants sub-millisecond reads for hot content. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the DB instance's storage size so that more of the popular articles are kept in memory.
Add an ElastiCache cache in front of the database using lazy loading (cache-aside) with TTLs.
Convert the database to Multi-AZ so that the standby instance answers all of the repeated reads.
Enable RDS Performance Insights only, and tune the slowest queries that it reports.
questions.correct_rationale: An in-memory cache serves repeated reads with sub-millisecond latency and offloads the database.
questions.distractor_summary: Storage size doesn't reduce CPU load, the Multi-AZ standby isn't used for reads, and Performance Insights diagnoses rather than fixes load.

questions.question: A gaming leaderboard reads the same DynamoDB items millions of times per minute and needs microsecond read latency. The team doesn't want to change its application logic for cache management significantly. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase provisioned read capacity only, so reads are served from the table.
Use DynamoDB global tables so that the reads are served from the replica Regions.
An ElastiCache for Memcached cluster with custom caching code in the application.
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), using the API-compatible DAX client.
questions.correct_rationale: DAX is an in-memory cache for DynamoDB that provides microsecond reads with minimal code changes.
questions.distractor_summary: More read capacity doesn't reach microsecond latency, global tables address multi-Region needs, and a separate cache requires custom logic.

questions.question: A reporting workload runs heavy read queries against an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL database, slowing down transactional writes. Reports can tolerate a few seconds of replication lag. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create RDS read replicas and direct the reporting queries to them.
Enable Multi-AZ and send the reports to the standby instance.
Increase the backup retention period of the database.
Run the reports on the primary during business hours only.
questions.correct_rationale: Read replicas offload read traffic asynchronously, which suits reports that tolerate slight lag.
questions.distractor_summary: The Multi-AZ DB instance standby can't serve reads, backup retention doesn't affect load, and running reports on the primary causes the problem.

questions.question: A SaaS application's relational database load varies unpredictably from near idle to very high within minutes. The company wants a MySQL-compatible database that scales capacity automatically in fine-grained increments without manual instance resizing or connection drops. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon RDS for MySQL with a large fixed instance sized for the peak.
Amazon Redshift Serverless, scaling the data warehouse with query load.
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2, which scales capacity up and down within minutes.
Amazon DynamoDB on-demand, after converting the schema to a key-value model.
questions.correct_rationale: Aurora Serverless v2 scales database capacity automatically in small increments based on load, with MySQL and PostgreSQL compatibility.
questions.distractor_summary: A fixed instance can't adapt, Redshift is a data warehouse, and DynamoDB isn't relational or MySQL-compatible.

questions.question: An IoT application stores sensor readings in DynamoDB with the partition key `sensorType`. There are only five sensor types, and most writes go to one type, causing throttling even though total provisioned capacity is sufficient. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the provisioned write capacity tenfold across the whole table and its partitions.
A high-cardinality partition key such as sensorId, with a timestamp sort key.
Enable DAX in front of the table to absorb the write traffic from the sensors.
Enable DynamoDB Streams to spread the writes across the partitions of the table.
questions.correct_rationale: Low-cardinality partition keys create hot partitions, and a high-cardinality key distributes writes across partitions.
questions.distractor_summary: More capacity doesn't fix skew efficiently, DAX caches reads, and Streams capture changes.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table of orders uses `orderId` as its partition key. A new feature requires querying all orders for a given customer sorted by order date, efficiently and at scale. Scans are currently used and are slow and expensive. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the table's read capacity and keep using scans filtered by the customer ID.
Export the table to S3 and query it with Athena for each request that arrives.
Create a local secondary index on the existing table with customerId as its partition key and orderDate as the sort key.
A global secondary index with customerId as partition key and orderDate as sort key, queried with Query.
questions.correct_rationale: A GSI provides an alternate key structure for efficient queries by customer and date.
questions.distractor_summary: Scans remain inefficient, Athena isn't suited to per-request application queries, and LSIs must be created at table creation and share the table's partition key.

questions.question: A retail company wants to run complex analytical SQL queries across petabytes of historical sales data, joining large fact and dimension tables, with fast performance for BI dashboards. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon Redshift, provisioned or Serverless, with columnar storage and massively parallel processing.
Amazon RDS for MySQL, scaled to the largest instance class with read replicas for dashboard queries.
Amazon DynamoDB with global secondary indexes on the sales tables to support the join queries.
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, caching the sales tables in memory so dashboards read from the cache.
questions.correct_rationale: Redshift is a columnar, MPP data warehouse optimized for complex analytics at petabyte scale.
questions.distractor_summary: RDS MySQL is built for OLTP, DynamoDB is key-value, and ElastiCache is an in-memory cache.

questions.question: An e-commerce site needs full-text product search with relevance ranking, typo tolerance, faceted filtering, and autocomplete over 20 million products that are stored in DynamoDB. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: DynamoDB scans with filter expressions run against the products table for each one of the searches.
Amazon Athena queries on the exported data, with the results returned to the website for each search.
Amazon OpenSearch Service, with the index kept updated from DynamoDB through zero-ETL or Streams.
Amazon RDS full-text indexes on a copy of the product catalog stored in a MySQL database instance.
questions.correct_rationale: OpenSearch provides full-text search with relevance, fuzzy matching, facets, and autocomplete, and it can be synchronized from DynamoDB. Scans are slow and lack search features, Athena isn't designed for interactive search, and RDS full-text features are limited at this scale.

questions.question: A bank wants to detect fraud rings by analyzing relationships between accounts, devices, phone numbers, and addresses, running queries that traverse several levels of connections in milliseconds. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with many joins across the account and device tables.
Amazon Neptune, a graph database built for relationship queries across connected data.
Amazon Redshift with the relationship tables joined in analytical queries.
Amazon Timestream, with the account events stored as time series records.
questions.correct_rationale: Neptune is a graph database optimized for traversing highly connected data.
questions.distractor_summary: Relational joins across many hops become slow, Redshift targets analytics, and Timestream stores time-series data.

questions.question: A company runs a self-managed MongoDB cluster storing JSON documents for a content platform. It wants a fully managed, MongoDB-compatible document database on AWS with high availability across AZs and minimal application changes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon DynamoDB, with the application rewritten to use the DynamoDB document APIs instead.
Amazon Keyspaces, with the application rewritten to use Cassandra Query Language.
RDS for MySQL with JSON columns, with the documents stored in a table.
Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility), a managed document database.
questions.correct_rationale: DocumentDB is a managed document database that supports MongoDB APIs and drivers, with replicas across AZs.
questions.distractor_summary: DynamoDB and Keyspaces use different APIs, and MySQL JSON columns require application changes.

questions.question: A media website hosted in `us-east-1` serves images, videos, and dynamic pages to users worldwide. Users far from the Region experience slow load times. The company wants to reduce latency for both static and dynamic content and reduce load on its origin. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: CloudFront in front of the origin, caching static content at the edge and accelerating dynamic content.
Deploy larger EC2 instances in us-east-1 so that the pages are generated faster for users who are far away.
Use Route 53 simple routing with several records to send each of the users to the closest origin server.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for all of the content, including the dynamic pages from the web servers.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudFront caches content close to users and uses optimized connections back to the origin for dynamic requests.
questions.distractor_summary: Larger instances don't reduce geographic latency, simple routing doesn't cache, and Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads to S3 rather than content delivery.

questions.question: A high-frequency data processing application on EC2 needs very high packets per second and low network jitter between instances. Current instances don't use enhanced networking. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Use Classic Load Balancers between the instances to spread the packet processing load.
Increase the EBS volume size so that the instances receive more network throughput.
Use instance types with ENA enhanced networking, with the ENA driver enabled and higher bandwidth.
Place the instances in different Regions so that the network traffic is spread out more widely over time.
questions.correct_rationale: ENA-based enhanced networking provides higher bandwidth, higher PPS, and lower latency and jitter.
questions.distractor_summary: Load balancers add hops, EBS size doesn't affect network performance, and multi-Region placement increases latency.

questions.question: A company transfers several terabytes daily between its data center and AWS for analytics. Its internet-based VPN has inconsistent throughput and latency that disrupt processing windows. The company wants consistent, high-bandwidth private connectivity. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Add more Site-to-Site VPN tunnels over the internet and spread the traffic across the tunnels.
AWS Direct Connect with a dedicated or hosted connection sized for the bandwidth.
Amazon CloudFront in front of the data center, caching the analytics data at the edge.
S3 Transfer Acceleration for all of the traffic between the data center and the AWS Region.
questions.correct_rationale: Direct Connect provides dedicated private connectivity with consistent performance and high bandwidth.
questions.distractor_summary: More VPN tunnels still use the internet, CloudFront is a CDN, and Transfer Acceleration only speeds S3 transfers over the internet.

questions.question: A company has 120 VPCs across multiple accounts and needs them all to communicate with each other and with on-premises networks through Direct Connect. Managing VPC peering connections has become unworkable. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Create more VPC peering connections in a full mesh between the VPCs and the data center.
Use AWS PrivateLink for all of the VPC-to-VPC traffic and the on-premises traffic.
Use a single VPC for all of the accounts and share the subnets with each account.
Transit Gateway as a central hub with all VPCs attached through AWS RAM and a Direct Connect gateway.
questions.correct_rationale: Transit Gateway provides scalable hub-and-spoke connectivity for many VPCs and on-premises networks.
questions.distractor_summary: A full peering mesh doesn't scale, PrivateLink exposes individual services rather than full network connectivity, and a single VPC removes account isolation.

questions.question: Two VPCs in the same Region, owned by different teams, need high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity between an application and a database. There are no other VPCs involved, and CIDR ranges don't overlap. What is the simplest, most cost-effective solution?
options: A VPC peering connection, with route table entries in both VPCs.
A Transit Gateway with a VPC attachment from each VPC and routes in each VPC's route table.
A Site-to-Site VPN between the two VPCs, with virtual private gateways and tunnels on each side.
Traffic routed over the public internet between the application and the database public endpoints.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC peering directly connects two VPCs with low latency and no per-hour attachment costs.
questions.distractor_summary: A Transit Gateway adds cost and complexity for two VPCs, VPN adds overhead, and the internet is less secure and less consistent.

questions.question: A CloudFront distribution needs to perform lightweight request manipulations, such as URL rewrites, header normalization for better cache hit ratios, and simple redirects, for millions of requests per second with minimal latency and cost. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Lambda@Edge for all of the request manipulations, running in the Regional edge caches.
An ALB listener rule at the origin that rewrites the URLs and normalizes the headers.
CloudFront Functions associated with viewer request events for lightweight rewrites.
An EC2 proxy in each Region, rewriting the requests before the origin.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript at edge locations with sub-millisecond startup and low cost, ideal for simple header and URL manipulations at high scale.
questions.distractor_summary: Lambda@Edge suits heavier logic at higher cost, origin rules happen after the edge, and EC2 proxies add latency and management.

questions.question: A company connects 30 branch offices in different countries to AWS with Site-to-Site VPN over the internet. Some branches experience high latency and packet loss on the public internet path to the AWS Region. What should the solutions architect recommend to improve VPN performance without Direct Connect?
options: Use larger EC2 instances in the VPC and add more VPN tunnels so that the gateway can process more traffic.
Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN using Global Accelerator, on VPN connections attached to a Transit Gateway.
Use CloudFront for the VPN traffic, so that packets reach the nearest AWS edge location.
Increase the VPN tunnel MTU so that more data is carried in each packet that is sent.
questions.correct_rationale: Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN routes traffic to the nearest AWS edge location and over the AWS global network, improving consistency.
questions.distractor_summary: Instance size doesn't affect the internet path, CloudFront doesn't carry VPN traffic, and higher MTU can worsen fragmentation.

questions.question: A company serves a static website from an S3 bucket through CloudFront. Security requires that the bucket not be publicly accessible, while performance requires all users to be served through CloudFront. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Make the bucket public with S3 static website hosting, and use the website endpoint as the CloudFront origin for the site.
Use a presigned URL for every object, generated by the web application for each of the viewer requests that arrive at the site.
Place the bucket behind an ALB, and let CloudFront send the requests to the load balancer.
CloudFront origin access control (OAC) with a bucket policy allowing only the distribution, Block Public Access on.
questions.correct_rationale: OAC lets CloudFront access a private bucket, and the bucket policy limits access to that distribution.
questions.distractor_summary: Public buckets violate security, presigned URLs for every object are impractical, and ALBs can't use S3 buckets as targets.

questions.question: Applications in VPCs must resolve hostnames in the on-premises `corp.example.com` domain, and on-premises servers must resolve names in Route 53 private hosted zones, over an existing Direct Connect connection. The company wants a managed solution without running DNS servers on EC2. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints for on-premises queries and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules.
Public hosted zones holding the internal names, resolvable from both the on-premises network and the VPCs.
Hosts files on every server in the VPCs, updated by a script whenever the on-premises DNS records change.
A NAT gateway for the DNS traffic, with the on-premises DNS servers reached through the gateway's elastic IP.
questions.correct_rationale: Route 53 Resolver endpoints provide managed hybrid DNS resolution in both directions.
questions.distractor_summary: Public zones expose internal names, hosts files don't scale, and NAT gateways don't resolve DNS.

questions.question: A company collects clickstream data from its website and wants it delivered to S3 in near real time, converted to Apache Parquet, buffered into larger files, and optionally loaded into Redshift, without writing or managing consumer applications. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Kinesis Data Streams with custom EC2 consumers writing Parquet files to S3.
An SQS queue with Lambda writing the individual records to S3 as JSON.
Amazon Data Firehose with record format conversion to Parquet and delivery to S3.
AWS DataSync tasks that copy the clickstream files into S3 every few minutes.
questions.correct_rationale: Data Firehose is a fully managed delivery service that buffers, converts formats, and loads data into S3, Redshift, and other destinations without consumer code.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom consumers require management, per-record writes create many small files, and DataSync transfers files between storage systems.

questions.question: A ride-sharing company streams trip events and needs to compute rolling five-minute aggregates per city, detect anomalies, and handle late-arriving events with exactly-once state semantics, in near real time. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon Athena queries run every five minutes against the data in S3, written by the stream.
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink consuming from Kinesis Data Streams or MSK.
AWS Glue batch jobs that run every hour over the trip events.
Amazon Redshift COPY commands run every minute against the trip files.
questions.correct_rationale: Managed Service for Apache Flink processes streams with windowing, event-time handling, and stateful exactly-once semantics.
questions.distractor_summary: Scheduled Athena queries and Glue batches aren't real time, and repeated COPY commands don't provide streaming analytics.

questions.question: A company's event pipeline is built on Apache Kafka, with dozens of producers and consumers using Kafka clients and Kafka Connect. It wants to move to AWS without rewriting clients and without managing Kafka brokers and ZooKeeper nodes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon SQS FIFO queues, with the producers and consumers rewritten to use the SQS APIs.
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, with all producers and consumers rewritten to use the Kinesis APIs.
Amazon SNS topics, with the consumers rewritten as subscribers that receive pushed messages.
Amazon MSK, optionally MSK Serverless, with MSK Connect so the Kafka clients keep working.
questions.correct_rationale: MSK runs Apache Kafka as a managed service compatible with existing clients and connectors.
questions.distractor_summary: SQS, SNS, and Kinesis require client rewrites to different APIs.

questions.question: A company lands raw CSV and JSON files from many sources in S3. It needs to discover schemas automatically, maintain a central metadata catalog, and run serverless ETL jobs that clean and convert data to Parquet for analytics. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Glue crawlers to populate the Data Catalog, and Glue ETL Spark jobs for transformations.
Amazon EC2 instances running custom Python scripts that infer each file's schema by hand.
Amazon RDS as a metadata store with the schemas entered manually for each of the sources.
Amazon Data Firehose for batch files already in S3, converting them as they arrive.
questions.correct_rationale: Glue crawlers infer schemas into the Data Catalog, and Glue ETL provides serverless Spark transformations.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom EC2 scripts require management, manual catalogs don't scale, and Firehose ingests streaming data rather than transforming files already in S3.

questions.question: Analysts run ad hoc SQL queries on 50 TB of log data stored in S3 as CSV files with Amazon Athena. Queries are slow and expensive because they scan all data, although most queries filter by date and select a few columns. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Load all of the data into Amazon RDS for MySQL and run the ad hoc SQL queries there instead.
Increase Athena's query concurrency limit so that the queries finish sooner for each of the analysts.
Convert the data to Parquet with compression and partition it by date, so Athena scans less.
Move the data to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval to reduce both the storage cost and the query cost.
questions.correct_rationale: Columnar compressed formats reduce scanned bytes for selected columns, and date partitioning prunes irrelevant data, improving speed and cost.
questions.distractor_summary: RDS isn't built for this analytics scale, concurrency doesn't reduce scanning, and Glacier storage isn't directly queryable by Athena.

questions.question: A company must migrate 60 TB of files from an on-premises NFS server to Amazon EFS and S3 over a 10 Gbps Direct Connect link, then keep them synchronized weekly until cutover, with data integrity validation and minimal scripting. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Snowball Edge devices ordered every week for the data.
AWS DataSync with an on-premises agent and scheduled tasks to EFS and S3.
rsync scripts run from an EC2 instance against the NFS export.
AWS Transfer Family servers exposing the NFS export over SFTP.
questions.correct_rationale: DataSync automates online transfers between on-premises storage and AWS services with scheduling, incremental copies, and integrity validation.
questions.distractor_summary: Weekly Snowball shipments are slow and unnecessary with a fast link, rsync scripts require maintenance, and Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTP endpoints.

questions.question: A mining company collects 80 TB of sensor and video data at a remote site with very limited connectivity. It needs to perform some local processing at the site and then move the data into S3. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS DataSync over the site's satellite link, scheduled for the hours when the link is least busy each day.
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration for the uploads over the satellite link from the remote site.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN over the satellite link, with the data sent to S3 through the tunnel.
Snowball Edge devices with local compute for preprocessing, shipped back to AWS for import into S3.
questions.correct_rationale: Snowball Edge provides rugged storage and edge compute for disconnected sites and offline transfer into S3.
questions.distractor_summary: Online transfer methods are limited by the poor connection, and VPN doesn't add bandwidth.

questions.question: Dozens of business partners send daily files using SFTP to a company's on-premises SFTP server, which is being retired. The company wants a fully managed SFTP endpoint that stores files directly in S3, with partner authentication, and without partners changing their clients. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Transfer Family with an SFTP-enabled server backed by S3, keeping the partners' clients.
An EC2 instance running an SFTP server, with the partners' files stored on an attached EBS volume.
Amazon S3 presigned URLs sent to the partners every day, with each partner changing their clients.
AWS DataSync agents installed at each partner location to copy the daily files.
questions.correct_rationale: Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS, and FTP endpoints that store files in S3 or EFS with flexible authentication, so partners keep using SFTP. An EC2 server requires management, presigned URLs change the partner workflow, and DataSync isn't an SFTP endpoint.

questions.question: A company is building a data lake on S3 used by Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR. Different analyst groups must see only specific databases, tables, columns, and rows, managed centrally rather than through complex S3 bucket policies. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: S3 bucket policies written for each prefix and for each of the analyst groups.
Separate S3 buckets for each analyst group, with the data copied into each bucket.
Lake Formation permissions, including column- and row-level security, on Glue Data Catalog resources.
IAM users with access keys for each analyst, with policies written for the tables.
questions.correct_rationale: Lake Formation centralizes fine-grained permissions for data lake tables, including column- and row-level controls enforced by integrated analytics services.
questions.distractor_summary: Bucket policies can't express column or row security, copying data creates drift, and access keys are a security risk.
