questions.question: A company stores 500 TB of user-generated content in S3 Standard. Access patterns are unpredictable: some objects go untouched for months and then suddenly become popular. The company wants to reduce storage costs automatically without retrieval fees or operational overhead. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Move all of the objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval to reduce the storage cost.
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which moves the objects between access tiers based on the access patterns.
Move all of the objects to S3 One Zone-IA to reduce the storage cost of all of the content.
Create a lifecycle rule that moves the objects to S3 Standard-IA after thirty days of age.
questions.correct_rationale: Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage, with no retrieval fees, which suits unpredictable access.
questions.distractor_summary: Glacier Flexible Retrieval adds retrieval delays and fees, One Zone-IA reduces resilience and charges retrievals, and fixed lifecycle rules can incur retrieval fees when old objects become popular.

questions.question: A company generates application logs in S3. Logs are accessed frequently for 30 days, occasionally for investigations for the next 60 days, rarely for up to six months, and must be deleted after seven years. Retrieval of logs older than six months can take up to 12 hours. What lifecycle configuration should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Keep all logs in S3 Standard for seven years, with a lifecycle rule that expires them after that.
Move logs to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately, and expire them after seven years of retention.
Move logs to S3 One Zone-IA after one day, keep them there, and expire them after seven years.
Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90, Deep Archive at 180, expire at seven years.
questions.correct_rationale: Tiered transitions match declining access frequency and acceptable retrieval times, and expiration removes data after retention.
questions.distractor_summary: Keeping everything in Standard overpays, immediate Deep Archive makes frequent early access impractical, and One Zone-IA reduces resilience and isn't cheapest for long-term archives.

questions.question: A cost review shows that an S3 bucket with versioning enabled is much larger than expected. Investigation reveals many noncurrent object versions from frequent overwrites and thousands of incomplete multipart uploads from failed transfers. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Disable versioning and delete the bucket, then recreate the bucket and copy the current objects back into it.
Add lifecycle rules that expire noncurrent versions after some days and abort incomplete multipart uploads.
Move the bucket to S3 One Zone-IA to reduce the storage cost of all of the noncurrent object versions in it.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so that the large number of versions is stored faster.
questions.correct_rationale: Lifecycle rules can remove old noncurrent versions and clean up incomplete multipart uploads that silently consume storage.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the bucket loses data, storage class changes don't remove waste, and Transfer Acceleration affects upload speed.

questions.question: A company with 300 buckets across 25 accounts wants organization-wide visibility into storage usage and activity trends, recommendations to reduce storage costs, and analysis of access patterns to decide when to move data to infrequent access tiers. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor only, which shows the storage usage of each bucket in each of the accounts.
CloudTrail data events for all of the buckets, with the logs queried in Athena for usage.
Manual reviews of each bucket in the console, repeated every month for each of the 25 accounts.
S3 Storage Lens with advanced metrics at organization level, plus Storage Class Analysis.
questions.correct_rationale: Storage Lens provides organization-wide usage and activity metrics with recommendations, and Storage Class Analysis evaluates access patterns to inform tiering.
questions.distractor_summary: Trusted Advisor offers limited S3 checks, CloudTrail data events are costly and not designed for storage analytics, and manual reviews don't scale.

questions.question: A cost audit finds hundreds of unattached EBS volumes left over from terminated instances and thousands of old manual snapshots. The company wants to remove the waste and automate snapshot creation and retention for its remaining volumes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Delete unneeded unattached volumes, clean up old snapshots, and use Data Lifecycle Manager policies for snapshots.
Convert all of the volumes to io2 so that the unattached volumes are billed at a lower rate in each month that follows.
Keep all of the volumes and snapshots for safety, and then review the bill again in a year.
Move all volumes to instance store so that the unattached volumes cost nothing at all.
questions.correct_rationale: Removing unused volumes and snapshots eliminates waste, and lifecycle policies automate creation and retention to prevent recurrence. io2 increases cost, keeping everything wastes money, and instance store is ephemeral.

questions.question: A company has 2,000 gp2 EBS volumes. Most volumes are sized larger than needed solely to get more IOPS. The company wants to reduce EBS costs without downtime or performance loss. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Convert the volumes to st1, which provides a lower cost per GB for the workloads running on these volumes.
Convert the volumes to sc1, which provides the lowest cost per GB for the workloads running on these volumes.
Modify the volumes to gp3 using Elastic Volumes, provisioning IOPS and throughput independently of size.
Move the data to S3 Standard and mount the buckets on the instances with a file gateway.
questions.correct_rationale: gp3 costs less per GB than gp2 and lets IOPS and throughput be set independently of size, and Elastic Volumes changes type without downtime.
questions.distractor_summary: HDD types reduce random I/O performance, and S3 isn't a block storage replacement.

questions.question: A company must keep monthly EBS snapshots of retired systems for seven years for compliance. These snapshots are rarely, if ever, restored, and a restore time of a day or more is acceptable. The company wants to lower snapshot storage costs. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Keep the snapshots in the standard snapshot tier, which stores them incrementally.
Move the snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive tier, billed at a lower rate for rarely used data.
Copy the snapshots to another Region, where the storage price is lower for the data.
Convert the snapshots into AMIs and deregister the AMIs when each seven-year period ends.
questions.correct_rationale: The EBS Snapshots Archive tier significantly reduces storage cost for rarely accessed snapshots, with longer restore times.
questions.distractor_summary: The standard tier costs more, cross-Region copies add cost, and AMIs don't reduce snapshot storage cost.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon EFS for a shared file system where most files aren't accessed after a few weeks, and a separate EFS file system for development data that can tolerate the loss of an AZ. The company wants to reduce EFS costs. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Migrate both file systems to EBS volumes, so that each instance has its own copy of the files.
Increase the provisioned throughput on both file systems so that the infrequently used files are served faster to users.
Move all of the files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive and mount the archive on the instances.
Enable EFS lifecycle management to Infrequent Access and Archive, with EFS One Zone for the development file system.
questions.correct_rationale: EFS lifecycle policies move cold files to lower-cost storage classes, and One Zone storage costs less for data that doesn't need multi-AZ resilience.
questions.distractor_summary: EBS isn't shared across instances, higher throughput increases cost, and Deep Archive isn't a mountable file system.

questions.question: A company spends steadily on compute, but its workloads frequently change between EC2 instance families and Regions, and some are moving to Fargate and Lambda. It wants a commitment-based discount that automatically applies across these changes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Compute Savings Plans, which apply across instance families and Regions.
Standard Reserved Instances for specific instance types.
Dedicated Hosts reserved for the families it uses.
Spot Instances for all workloads, interruptible or not.
questions.correct_rationale: Compute Savings Plans apply across instance families, sizes, Regions, operating systems, Fargate, and Lambda.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard RIs lock to specific attributes, Dedicated Hosts cost more, and Spot Instances aren't suitable for all workloads.

questions.question: A company runs a fleet of `m6i` instances in `eu-west-1` 24/7 for its production database tier and has no plans to change the instance family or Region for three years. It wants the largest possible discount. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Compute Savings Plans with a three-year term, which apply across instance families and Regions.
On-Demand Instances with Auto Scaling, so that capacity follows the load on the database tier.
EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the `m6i` family in `eu-west-1` with a three-year term.
Spot Instances for the whole database tier, with a fallback to On-Demand when capacity is reclaimed.
questions.correct_rationale: EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Standard RIs give the deepest discounts in exchange for committing to a specific instance family and Region.
questions.distractor_summary: Compute Savings Plans are more flexible but offer slightly lower discounts, On-Demand forgoes savings, and Spot isn't appropriate for a production database.

questions.question: A data analytics company runs large, fault-tolerant batch jobs that checkpoint progress and can be interrupted. It wants the lowest compute cost while minimizing interruptions. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: On-Demand Instances only, with the batch jobs started and stopped on demand each day by the scheduler.
Spot Instances diversified across instance types and AZs, with the price-capacity-optimized strategy.
Spot Instances of a single instance type in one AZ with the lowest-price allocation strategy, for all jobs.
Dedicated Instances for all of the jobs, with the capacity reserved for each of them.
questions.correct_rationale: Diversifying Spot capacity and using price-capacity-optimized allocation reduces interruptions while keeping costs low.
questions.distractor_summary: On-Demand costs more, a single pool with lowest price increases interruption risk, and Dedicated Instances are more expensive.

questions.question: A stateless web application runs in an Auto Scaling group. The company wants a guaranteed baseline of capacity for reliability and wants any capacity above that baseline to use the cheapest available option, accepting that the extra capacity may be interrupted. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: All On-Demand Instances in the group, sized for the full peak load of the application at all times.
All Spot Instances, with the group replacing each of the instances whenever the capacity is reclaimed.
Dedicated Hosts with Auto Scaling, with the hosts allocated for the baseline capacity of the group.
A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base and Spot above the base, across instance types.
questions.correct_rationale: Mixed instances policies combine a reliable On-Demand base with cheaper Spot capacity for scaling, diversified across types.
questions.distractor_summary: All On-Demand costs more, all Spot risks losing the baseline, and Dedicated Hosts are expensive.

questions.question: A company runs containerized Java and Python microservices on x86-based EC2 instances. The applications aren't tied to x86-specific binaries. The company wants better price performance without major changes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Migrate to Graviton-based instances after building multi-architecture arm64 container images and testing.
Move to larger x86 instances so that the services can handle more of the load.
Use Dedicated Hosts so that the services have a physical server for themselves.
Switch to burstable T2 instances so that idle periods cost less for the services.
questions.correct_rationale: Graviton-based instances generally offer better price performance for compatible workloads such as Java and Python.
questions.distractor_summary: Larger x86 instances increase cost, Dedicated Hosts are more expensive, and older burstable instances may throttle.

questions.question: A company has 800 EC2 instances whose sizes were chosen without performance data. It wants data-driven recommendations for downsizing or changing instance types based on actual CPU, memory, and network utilization, and it's willing to install the CloudWatch agent for memory metrics. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Double all of the instance sizes to be safe against performance problems at each peak.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor's security checks to get the sizing advice for the instances.
Use AWS Compute Optimizer, with memory metrics collected by the CloudWatch agent.
Use Amazon Inspector findings to find the instances that are oversized.
questions.correct_rationale: Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization metrics to recommend right-sized instance types, and memory data from the CloudWatch agent improves accuracy.
questions.distractor_summary: Doubling sizes increases waste, security checks don't address sizing, and Inspector scans for vulnerabilities.

questions.question: A company's development and test EC2 and RDS instances run 24/7, but developers work only weekdays from 8 AM to 6 PM. The company wants to reduce costs automatically without affecting production. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Purchase Reserved Instances for all of the development resources, using a one-year term with no upfront payment made.
Use AWS Instance Scheduler to stop tagged development instances outside working hours and start them each morning.
Convert all of the development instances to Dedicated Hosts, which are billed for each host instead of each instance.
Delete the development environments every night and have the developers rebuild them by hand every morning, using the runbook.
questions.correct_rationale: Scheduling stops and starts of non-production resources removes charges during idle hours.
questions.distractor_summary: Reservations charge for full-time capacity, Dedicated Hosts increase cost, and manual rebuilds waste engineering time.

questions.question: A company runs a small EC2 instance 24/7 that processes uploaded files. Uploads happen only about 200 times per day, and each takes a few seconds to process. The instance is idle more than 99% of the time. What should the solutions architect recommend to reduce costs?
options: Purchase a Reserved Instance for the EC2 instance for a one-year term.
Switch the instance to a larger size to process files faster.
Use an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of two instances.
Replace the instance with a Lambda function triggered by S3 upload events.
questions.correct_rationale: Lambda charges only for execution time, making it far cheaper for sporadic, short-lived processing.
questions.distractor_summary: A Reserved Instance still pays for idle time, a larger instance costs more, and two instances double idle costs.

questions.question: A company runs containerized, interruption-tolerant batch tasks on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. It wants to reduce the cost of these tasks significantly without managing EC2 instances. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Run the tasks using the Fargate Spot capacity provider, which uses spare capacity at a discount.
Move the tasks to ECS on On-Demand EC2 instances, which the team then patches and scales itself.
Increase the task CPU and memory so each batch task finishes faster and uses less run time.
Use Dedicated Hosts for the ECS container instances so the batch tasks run on isolated hardware.
questions.correct_rationale: Fargate Spot runs interruption-tolerant tasks on spare capacity at a discount, without managing instances.
questions.distractor_summary: EC2-based ECS adds instance management, larger tasks cost more, and Dedicated Hosts are expensive.

questions.question: A company placed all its EC2 workloads on Dedicated Hosts "for security," although only one application requires dedicated hardware because of a per-socket software license. Costs are high. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Keep all of the workloads on Dedicated Hosts, because the hosts physically isolate every one of the workloads.
Move all of the workloads, including the licensed application, to Spot Instances for a lower cost.
Keep only the licensed application on Dedicated Hosts and move the others to shared tenancy.
Move everything on-premises to avoid paying for Dedicated Hosts in AWS, then buy new servers.
questions.correct_rationale: Dedicated Hosts are needed only for specific licensing or compliance requirements, and shared tenancy is secure for most workloads at lower cost.
questions.distractor_summary: Keeping everything dedicated wastes money, Spot may break the licensed app's requirements and reliability, and moving on-premises ignores the targeted fix.

questions.question: A company runs hundreds of Lambda functions with default memory settings and x86_64 architecture. Its monthly Lambda bill is growing. It wants to reduce cost per invocation while maintaining performance. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the timeout for all of the functions so that the executions never fail early, then review the costs.
Use Lambda Power Tuning to find the best memory per function, and move compatible functions to arm64.
Enable provisioned concurrency for all of the functions so that every execution is fast.
Move all of the functions into a VPC so that the network traffic is cheaper.
questions.correct_rationale: Right-sizing memory balances speed and cost, and arm64 functions typically offer better price performance.
questions.distractor_summary: Longer timeouts don't reduce cost, provisioned concurrency adds cost unless needed for latency, and VPC placement doesn't reduce cost.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table supports a mature application with steady, predictable traffic that varies gradually between daytime and night. The table currently uses on-demand capacity, and costs are higher than expected. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling, and consider reserved capacity for the baseline.
Keep on-demand mode and add DAX in front of the table to reduce the number of billed read requests.
Move the table to Amazon RDS, which charges for the provisioned instance instead of the requests made.
Duplicate the table in another Region so that the traffic is shared across the two copies of the table.
questions.correct_rationale: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling is typically cheaper than on-demand for predictable workloads, and reserved capacity reduces baseline cost further.
questions.distractor_summary: DAX adds cost without addressing capacity pricing, migrating to RDS is a large change, and duplicating tables increases cost.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table stores 40 TB of historical order records that are rarely read, and storage makes up most of the table's cost. The application still needs the data online with the same performance when it is accessed. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Export the table to S3 Glacier and delete the table.
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode.
Change the table class to DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access.
Add a global secondary index on the order date.
questions.correct_rationale: The Standard-IA table class lowers storage costs for tables where storage dominates, while keeping data online with the same performance.
questions.distractor_summary: Exporting to Glacier removes online access, capacity mode doesn't change storage pricing, and a GSI adds storage cost.

questions.question: A DynamoDB table stores user session data that is useless after 24 hours. A nightly Lambda function scans the table and deletes expired items, consuming significant write capacity and adding cost. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the table's provisioned write capacity so that the nightly scan and deletes finish much sooner each night.
Enable DynamoDB TTL on an expiration timestamp attribute, so expired items are deleted without write capacity.
Move the sessions to Amazon RDS, where an index lets the nightly job delete the expired rows faster than a scan.
Run the cleanup Lambda function every hour so that fewer items are left in the table.
questions.correct_rationale: TTL deletes expired items automatically in the background without consuming write throughput.
questions.distractor_summary: More capacity increases cost, RDS adds complexity, and more frequent scans cost more.

questions.question: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL production database 24/7 on the same instance class and expects to continue for at least three years. It wants to reduce database costs with no architectural changes. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Stop the database each night and start it again each morning.
Migrate to DynamoDB and use on-demand capacity mode for all of the data.
Use Spot Instances for RDS to lower the hourly price of the instance.
Purchase RDS Reserved Instances for the instance class and Region.
questions.correct_rationale: RDS Reserved Instances offer significant discounts for steady, long-term database usage without architectural changes.
questions.distractor_summary: Stopping production databases causes outages, migrating to DynamoDB is a major redesign, and RDS doesn't run on Spot Instances.

questions.question: A company uses Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL Standard configuration for an I/O-intensive transactional workload. Cost analysis shows that I/O charges exceed 25% of its total Aurora spend and fluctuate unpredictably. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Switch the cluster to the Aurora I/O-Optimized configuration, which has no per-request I/O charges.
Migrate to RDS for PostgreSQL on gp2 storage, which bills for provisioned storage and baseline IOPS.
Add more Aurora Replicas, so that the read traffic is spread across more instances in the cluster.
Enable Aurora Backtrack, so that the cluster can be rewound to an earlier point without a restore.
questions.correct_rationale: Aurora I/O-Optimized removes per-request I/O charges in exchange for higher instance and storage pricing, making costs predictable and often lower for I/O-heavy workloads.
questions.distractor_summary: Migrating to RDS changes the platform, more replicas add cost, and Backtrack is a recovery feature.

questions.question: A company has 30 RDS development databases that are used only during business hours on weekdays. The team wants to minimize costs without deleting the databases. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Purchase Reserved Instances for all of the development databases, using a one-year term with no upfront payment.
Convert all of the development databases to Multi-AZ so that they stay available throughout all working hours.
Stop the RDS instances outside business hours on a schedule, or use Aurora Serverless v2 with low minimums.
Increase the instance sizes of the databases so that the developers can work faster during business hours.
questions.correct_rationale: Stopping instances removes compute charges during idle hours, and Aurora Serverless v2 scales down when idle, both reducing development costs.
questions.distractor_summary: Reservations and Multi-AZ increase or lock in costs, and larger instances cost more.

questions.question: A company's RDS for MySQL database is 8 TB and growing, driven mostly by historical records older than two years that are queried only for occasional analytics. Storage and instance costs are rising. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Increase the RDS instance size to handle the growing amount of data, and keep all of the historical records in RDS.
Add read replicas for the historical queries so that the primary database stores much less of the data overall.
Move the historical data to DynamoDB and query it with the DynamoDB APIs when needed.
Archive historical records to S3 in Parquet format and query them with Athena, keeping recent data in RDS.
questions.correct_rationale: Moving cold historical data to S3 and querying it with Athena reduces database storage and instance needs, charging only for queries run.
questions.distractor_summary: Bigger instances and replicas increase costs, and DynamoDB isn't suited to occasional analytical SQL on historical data.

questions.question: A marketing team runs analytics queries on a data warehouse a few hours per week, with long idle periods. The company currently runs a provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster 24/7. What should the solutions architect recommend to reduce costs?
options: Add more nodes to the provisioned cluster so that the queries run faster.
Use Redshift Serverless, paying only for the compute used while queries run.
Migrate the data warehouse to RDS for PostgreSQL to reduce costs.
Purchase Reserved Nodes for the cluster to lower the rate.
questions.correct_rationale: Redshift Serverless automatically provisions and scales compute and charges only for usage, which suits intermittent analytics.
questions.distractor_summary: More nodes and Reserved Nodes pay for idle capacity, and RDS isn't optimized for data warehousing.

questions.question: A company keeps daily backups of all databases for 10 years in AWS Backup with warm storage, even though compliance requires only monthly backups for long-term retention, and daily backups for 35 days. Backup storage costs are high. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Revise the backup plans to keep daily backups for 35 days and monthly backups for 10 years, with cold storage.
Stop taking backups of the databases and rely on the database snapshots taken by hand.
Move all of the backups to another Region so that the storage costs are lower there.
Increase the backup frequency to hourly so that fewer of the old backups are needed to meet compliance requirements.
questions.correct_rationale: Aligning retention with requirements and using cold storage for long-term backups reduces cost while staying compliant.
questions.distractor_summary: Stopping backups violates compliance, cross-Region copies add cost, and more frequent backups increase storage.

questions.question: Instances in private subnets send about 50 TB per month to S3 and DynamoDB through NAT gateways. The NAT gateway data processing charges are a large part of the network bill. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Replace the NAT gateways with NAT instances, which have no per-GB data processing charge applied to the traffic.
Move the instances to public subnets so that all of the traffic leaves through the internet gateway directly.
Create S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints in the private route tables, avoiding NAT processing charges.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the buckets that the instances write to.
questions.correct_rationale: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route traffic privately without NAT gateway data processing charges.
questions.distractor_summary: NAT instances require management and still route through them, public subnets increase exposure, and Transfer Acceleration adds cost.

questions.question: A microservices application exchanges hundreds of terabytes per month between services placed randomly across three AZs. Cost analysis shows large inter-AZ data transfer charges. The services still need to survive the loss of an AZ. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Place all of the services in a single AZ so that the traffic between the services never crosses an AZ boundary again.
Route all of the traffic between the services through a NAT gateway so that the data transfer is charged at a lower rate.
Replace the load balancer with a Classic Load Balancer so that the cross-zone charges are removed for the services.
Keep AZ resilience, but prefer AZ-local routing for chatty calls and disable needless cross-zone load balancing.
questions.correct_rationale: AZ-affinity routing reduces cross-AZ transfer while retaining multi-AZ resilience.
questions.distractor_summary: A single AZ sacrifices availability, NAT gateways add charges, and changing load balancer types doesn't address cross-AZ traffic.

questions.question: A company serves 500 TB per month of images and videos directly from S3 and EC2 to users worldwide. Data transfer out charges are the largest item on its bill, and much of the content is requested repeatedly. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for the downloads, which speeds up the delivery to the users.
Serve the content through CloudFront, which caches at edge locations and reduces origin data transfer.
Move the content to S3 Glacier to lower the storage cost of the images and videos.
Use larger EC2 instances so that the content is delivered faster to the users worldwide.
questions.correct_rationale: CloudFront caches repeated requests at the edge, reducing origin load and data transfer, and there's no charge for data transfer from AWS origins to CloudFront.
questions.distractor_summary: Transfer Acceleration adds cost for uploads, Glacier is for archives, and larger instances don't reduce transfer charges.

questions.question: A company transfers 300 TB per month from AWS to its on-premises data center over the internet, incurring high data transfer out charges. It also needs more consistent performance. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Use Direct Connect, which has lower data transfer out rates than the internet and steady performance.
Use Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, which encrypts the traffic and lowers the data transfer rates a lot.
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration, which routes the transfers over the AWS edge network at a lower cost to the company.
Use Amazon CloudFront for all of the transfers to the data center, caching the files at the edge locations.
questions.correct_rationale: Data transferred out over Direct Connect is priced lower than internet data transfer, and the dedicated connection offers consistent performance.
questions.distractor_summary: VPN still uses internet transfer pricing, Transfer Acceleration adds charges, and CloudFront isn't designed for bulk transfers to a single data center.

questions.question: A company has only two VPCs in the same Region that exchange about 400 TB per month. They're connected through a Transit Gateway, and per-GB data processing charges are significant. No other VPCs or on-premises networks are involved. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Add a second Transit Gateway so that the traffic is split between the two gateways.
Route the traffic through the internet gateways so that the Transit Gateway data processing charges are avoided.
Replace the Transit Gateway connection with VPC peering, which has no per-GB data processing charges.
Use AWS PrivateLink for all of the traffic between the two VPCs in the Region.
questions.correct_rationale: For a small number of VPCs with high traffic volume, VPC peering avoids Transit Gateway data processing charges.
questions.distractor_summary: A second Transit Gateway doubles costs, internet routing adds transfer charges and risk, and PrivateLink charges per GB and exposes services rather than full networks.

questions.question: A company has 60 VPCs, each with its own set of 10 interface VPC endpoints for services such as Secrets Manager, KMS, and SSM. The hourly endpoint charges have become significant. The VPCs are already connected through a Transit Gateway. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Delete all of the interface endpoints and route the traffic to the services through NAT gateways in each VPC.
Replace the interface endpoints with gateway endpoints for all of the services in each of the VPCs.
Create the endpoints in every subnet of every VPC, and share the endpoint policies between the VPCs.
Centralize the interface endpoints in a shared services VPC, resolved from other VPCs through Route 53 private hosted zones and Transit Gateway.
questions.correct_rationale: Centralizing interface endpoints reduces the number of hourly-billed endpoints, and private hosted zones let spokes resolve them over the Transit Gateway.
questions.distractor_summary: NAT routing adds per-GB charges and internet paths, gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB, and more endpoints increase costs.

questions.question: Finance wants to analyze AWS costs by team, application, and environment, including network and data transfer costs, and see trends over the past year with forecasts. Resources are tagged inconsistently. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Review the monthly invoice PDF each month and split the totals by team in a spreadsheet kept by the finance team.
Define a tagging strategy with tag policies, activate cost allocation tags, and group costs in Cost Explorer.
Use CloudTrail to analyze the costs of each team, application, and environment by counting all of the API calls.
Create a separate AWS account for every single resource, so that each of the resources has its own monthly bill.
questions.correct_rationale: Consistent, activated cost allocation tags enable Cost Explorer to group costs and forecast trends.
questions.distractor_summary: Invoices lack this breakdown, CloudTrail records API activity rather than costs, and an account per resource is impractical.

questions.question: A company gives teams sandbox accounts for experimentation. It wants alerts when a sandbox account's spending reaches 80% of its monthly limit and automatic action at 100%, such as stopping EC2 instances or applying a restrictive policy. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: AWS Budgets with alerts at 80% and budget actions at 100% that stop instances or apply an SCP.
Cost Explorer reports reviewed by each team every month for the sandbox accounts.
CloudWatch alarms on CPU utilization that notify the team when the instances are busy.
AWS Trusted Advisor checks that report the spending of each sandbox account weekly.
questions.correct_rationale: AWS Budgets can send alerts at thresholds and run budget actions such as stopping instances or applying policies.
questions.distractor_summary: Monthly reviews are too slow, CPU alarms don't track spending, and Trusted Advisor provides recommendations rather than budget enforcement.

questions.question: A company stores its 200 TB data lake in an S3 bucket in `us-east-1`, but runs its EMR processing clusters in `us-west-2` because of a historical decision. Inter-Region data transfer charges are high. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration so that the data reaches the clusters in us-west-2 faster.
Replicate the data to us-west-2 with S3 Cross-Region Replication, keeping the buckets in sync.
Run the processing in us-east-1, the same Region as the data, where S3-to-EC2 transfer is free.
Use CloudFront between S3 and EMR so that the data is cached close to the clusters.
questions.correct_rationale: Co-locating compute with data in the same Region avoids inter-Region transfer charges.
questions.distractor_summary: Transfer Acceleration adds cost, replication still incurs transfer and duplicate storage costs, and CloudFront isn't intended for this processing path.

questions.question: A large enterprise wants to perform detailed chargeback across 200 accounts, analyzing line-item costs including data transfer by resource, and building custom dashboards with SQL. What should the solutions architect recommend?
options: The Billing console's bill details page only, exported by each account owner at the end of every single month.
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks, reviewed by the finance team for each one of the 200 accounts.
Amazon CloudWatch billing alarms, created in each account for the line-item charges.
Configure AWS Data Exports for the CUR 2.0 at the organization level, queried with Athena and QuickSight.
questions.correct_rationale: The Cost and Usage Report provides the most detailed line-item billing data, and Athena and QuickSight enable SQL analysis and dashboards.
questions.distractor_summary: The bill details page lacks line-item analysis, Trusted Advisor offers recommendations, and billing alarms only alert on thresholds.
